front: What was the impact of Presidential Reconstruction on African American rights?
p1: Johnson issued mass pardons to Southern whites → Confederate land returned → '40 acres and a mule' never realised.
p2: Black Codes introduced by Southern states → restricted movement, labour, property rights → de facto re-enslavement.
p3: Johnson actively opposed 14th and 15th Amendments → vetoed both → Congress overruled him.

front: What were the key achievements of Radical Reconstruction?
p1: 14th Amendment (1868) → citizenship + equal protection. 15th Amendment (1870) → voting rights for Black men.
p2: Reconstruction Act (1867) → South divided into military districts → Black Codes removed → elections enforced.
p3: 1,500+ African Americans held public office → 22 in Congress → Blanche Bruce: full Senate term for Mississippi.

front: Why did Reconstruction fail?
p1: Hayes–Tilden Compromise (1877) → federal troops withdrawn → 'Redeemer' governments retook the South.
p2: Deaths of Sumner and Stevens + Panic of 1873 → Northern attention shifts → Radical Republican majority diluted.
p3: Slaughterhouse Case (1873) → civil rights ruled a state issue → Supreme Court undermined 14th Amendment.

front: What was the impact of Jim Crow laws on African Americans?
p1: Spread across South from 1877 → segregated schools, transport, hospitals, parks, restaurants, churches.
p2: Voter suppression from 1890 → literacy tests, poll taxes, grandfather clauses → Mississippi Black voter registration: 90% (1867) → 6% (1892).
p3: Plessy v Ferguson (1896) → 'separate but equal' constitutional → gave legal cover to all Jim Crow legislation.

front: What was the significance of the Wilmington Coup (1898)?
p1: White supremacists violently overthrew the biracial elected government of Wilmington, North Carolina.
p2: Showed that even legitimate political power could be destroyed by organised white violence without federal protection.
p3: Mississippi v Williams (1898) same year → Supreme Court ruled voter suppression didn't violate 15th Amendment → over 90% disenfranchised by 1900.

front: What was the significance of Booker T. Washington?
p1: Atlanta Compromise (1895) → accepted social segregation in exchange for economic self-improvement → critics saw this as legitimising Jim Crow and abandoning political rights.
p2: Tuskegee Institute (1881) → trained 1,500 Black students in practical skills annually → Negro Business League (1900) → 600 chapters → 50,000+ Black-owned businesses by 1890s → first Black informal presidential advisor (Roosevelt, 1901).
p3: Du Bois argued Washington sacrificed political and social rights for economic gains → founded Niagara Movement (1905) in direct opposition → later NAACP (1909) → exposed limits of accommodation strategy.

front: What were the criticisms of Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise?
p1: Du Bois argued the Atlanta Compromise (1895) sacrificed political and social rights for economic gains — Washington's acceptance of segregation legitimised Jim Crow. Du Bois founded the Niagara Movement (1905) in direct opposition, demanding full civil and political rights.
p2: William Monroe Trotter: Washington's autocratic control of Black organisations ('Tuskegee Machine') — he controlled Black newspapers, charities and political appointments and was suspicious of critics. Ida B. Wells criticised his silence on lynching.
p3: Niagara Movement (1905) → directly led to the NAACP (1909)

front: What was the strategy and significance of the NAACP?
p1: Founded 1909 → Du Bois, Ida B. Wells + white progressives → legal litigation + political pressure strategy.
p2: Key victories: US v Guinn (1915) → grandfather clauses unconstitutional. Smith v Allwright (1944) → all-white primaries banned → Black voter registration 2% (1940) → 12% (1947).
p3: Brown v Board (1954) → Thurgood Marshall proved $43/yr Black vs $179/yr white → 'separate but equal' overturned. Little Rock Nine (1957) organised.

front: What was the significance of Marcus Garvey and UNIA?
p1: Founded UNIA New York branch (1917) → The Negro World newspaper → 200,000 weekly readers. Black Star Line (1919) → 'Back to Africa' movement.
p2: UNIA reached 4 million members by early 1920s → largest Black mass movement in history → Black nationalism + Pan-Africanism.
p3: 'Garvey must go' campaign (1922) after meeting KKK → deported to Jamaica (1927) for mail fraud → federal government action ended movement.

front: What was the role of State Governments in resisting desegregation?
p1: 'State Rights' ideology → argued states should manage affairs without federal interference → used to block civil rights enforcement.
p2: Massive resistance to Brown (1954) → Virginia closed all public schools rather than integrate → 300+ private 'segregation academies' founded.
p3: Wallace: 'segregation today, tomorrow, forever' → stood in University of Alabama doorway 1963. Faubus deployed National Guard against Little Rock Nine (1957).

front: What was the New Deal's impact on African American political rights?
p1: FDR created informal 'Black Cabinet' → led by Mary McLeod Bethune → influenced New Deal programmes for Black Americans.
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt advocated for civil rights + supported anti-lynching bills. African Americans began voting Democratic in large numbers → major long-term political shift.
p3: Anti-Communist Red Scare → organisations improving AA rights suspected of communism → Du Bois surveilled + harassed → CIO lost funding.

front: What was the significance of the Warren Court (1953–1969)?
p1: Warren Court (1953–69) → considered most liberal Supreme Court in US history → transformed federal protection of civil rights through judicial activism
p2: Brown v Board (1954) → overturned Plessy — 'separate but equal' unconstitutional in education → Brown II (1955): desegregation 'with all deliberate speed'
p3: Browder v Gayle (1956) → segregated buses unconstitutional → triggered end of Montgomery Bus Boycott → Boynton v Virginia (1960) → segregation on interstate buses unconstitutional

front: What was the impact of Brown v Board of Education (1954)?
p1: Thurgood Marshall proved Southern states spent $43/yr on Black students vs $179/yr white → Supreme Court overturned 'separate but equal'.
p2: Theoretically impacted 9 million Black children in the South → but no de facto change immediately → by 1964, 98% still attended segregated schools.
p3: Triggered 'massive resistance' across the South → Virginia closed schools → 300+ segregation academies founded → exposed limits of legal victories.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the SCLC?
p1: Founded 1957 → led by Martin Luther King → non-violent direct action → used media + moral pressure to force federal response.
p2: Birmingham Campaign (1963) → Bull Connor's violence vs peaceful protesters → broadcast nationwide → Kennedy announces moral duty to act → Civil Rights Act 1964.
p3: Selma March (1965) → 50% Black population, 1% electorate → Bloody Sunday broadcast nationally → directly led to Voting Rights Act 1965.

front: What was the strategy and significance of SNCC?
p1: Founded 1960 → grassroots, student-led → more radical than SCLC → organised sit-ins, Freedom Rides, voter registration drives.
p2: Selma March (1965) → John Lewis led marchers onto Edmund Pettus Bridge → 'Bloody Sunday' → Voting Rights Act.
p3: 1966 under Stokely Carmichael → rejected non-violence + integration → embraced Black Power → 'Black Power' slogan coined.

front: What was the Albany Campaign (1962) and why did it fail?
p1: SCLC and King targeted Albany, Georgia → Police Chief Laurie Pritchett used non-violent policing → denied King media images of brutality.
p2: No single dramatic confrontation → media lost interest → federal government had no reason to intervene → no legislation resulted.
p3: Key lesson → non-violent direct action only worked when it provoked visible repression on camera → shaped Birmingham Campaign strategy.

front: What were the Greensboro Sit-ins (1960) and why were they significant?
p1: 4 Black students sat at 'white-only' lunch counter in Greensboro, NC → spontaneous non-violent direct action.
p2: Over 70,000 students engaged in sit-ins across the South co-ordinated by SNCC → more than 1,000 businesses desegregated lunch counters.
p3: Demonstrated power of youth-led spontaneous protest → led to founding of SNCC → showed NAACP's legal approach could be complemented by direct action.

front: What were the Freedom Rides (1961) and what did they achieve?
p1: CORE + SNCC → Black and white activists rode interstate buses from Washington D.C. into the Deep South → testing Boynton v Virginia (1960).
p2: Met with violent mobs including fire-bombings in Alabama → national outrage → federal government forced to respond.
p3: Attorney General enforced desegregation of interstate public transport → demonstrated that federal pressure could be forced through confrontation.

front: What was the significance of the Birmingham Campaign (1963)?
p1: King + SCLC targeted Birmingham → Bull Connor used police dogs + fire hoses against peaceful protesters including children → images broadcast worldwide.
p2: Kennedy announced America had a 'moral duty' to intervene → directly led to Civil Rights Act 1964.
p3: Baptist Church bombings (1963) → KKK killed four young girls → no convictions → highlighted state government complicity in racial terror.

front: What was the significance of the March on Washington (1963)?
p1: 250,000 marched for jobs and freedom → King's 'I Have a Dream' speech → largest civil rights demonstration in US history.
p2: Organised by Randolph + Rustin → brought together NAACP, SCLC, SNCC, CORE, NUL → demonstrated broad coalition.
p3: Malcolm X dismissed it as a 'farce' → highlighted divisions between integrationist and nationalist wings of the movement.

front: What was the impact of the Civil Rights Act (1964)?
p1: Removed all Jim Crow segregation across the South → prohibited employment discrimination based on race.
p2: Pushed through by LBJ using 'Johnson treatment' → most significant federal civil rights legislation since Reconstruction.
p3: Limitations → did not address de facto segregation in the North → did not solve economic inequality → enforcement remained weak in many states.

front: What happened during the Selma March and what did it achieve?
p1: Selma: 50% Black population but only 1% of electorate → SCLC + SNCC march to expose voter suppression.
p2: Bloody Sunday → John Lewis led marchers → violent police attack on Edmund Pettus Bridge → broadcast nationwide.
p3: Directly led to Voting Rights Act (1965) → banned all voter suppression → Mississippi Black voter registration: 6% (1964) → 60% (1969).

front: What were Malcolm X's key ideas and the Nation of Islam?
p1: NOI → Black nationalism + separatism → rejected integration → 'by any means necessary' → self-defence against white supremacy.
p2: NOI grew from 400 members (1952) → 40,000 (1960) under Malcolm X → addressed Northern urban poverty King's movement neglected.
p3: Post-Hajj (1964) → Malcolm X adopted more inclusive vision → broke from NOI → assassinated by NOI members 1965 → became martyr for Black Power.

front: What were the key ideas of Stokely Carmichael and Black Power?
p1: 1966 → took over SNCC → rejected non-violence + integration → coined 'Black Power' slogan during Meredith March.
p2: Black Power = self-determination, Black pride, economic self-sufficiency, community control — not dependence on white liberals.
p3: Alienated white allies + moderate African Americans → CORE lost white funding 1969 → weakened cross-racial coalition that had passed 1964/65 legislation.

front: Why did Black Power rise to prominence in the late 1960s?
p1: Failures of CRM in North → SCLC/NAACP focused on Southern desegregation → Northern urban communities still faced poverty + police violence. King's Chicago (1966) failed.
p2: Vietnam War → African Americans disproportionately drafted → returned radicalised → war severed King–LBJ relationship → media attention shifted.
p3: Long Hot Summers → Watts (1965) $40m damage → 150 riots (1967) → showed non-violence couldn't address systemic Northern inequality.

front: What was the impact of Nixon's and Reagan's policies on African Americans?
p1: Nixon's 'Law and Order' (1968) → War on Drugs → disproportionately targeted Black communities. Reagan (1981–89) → welfare cuts deepened economic disparities
p2: Supreme Court became increasingly conservative under Reagan → affirmative action weakened → Bakke (1978) precedent extended. Reagan and Bush labelled affirmative action 'reverse discrimination' and reduced federal enforcement.
p3: By 1992 → 25% of Black men in prison, on parole or probation

front: What was the political position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: 8,000+ African Americans held public office → Congressional Black Caucus: 36 members → Thurgood Marshall (1967–91) first Black Supreme Court Justice. Douglas Wilder first Black governor (Virginia, 1989).
p2: Voter turnout 54% vs 61% white → unofficial suppression continued → gerrymandering + insufficient polling locations in Black areas.
p3: Jesse Jackson's 1984 + 1988 presidential campaigns won 7 million votes → but never official Democrat candidate → no Black presidential or VP candidate in the period.

front: What was the impact of the Freedmen's Bureau?
p1: Established 1865 → helped create 1,000+ Black schools → 250,000 enrolled → founded Howard University (1867), one of first HBCUs.
p2: Distributed 21 million rations of food to freedmen → provided basic housing, medical care and legal support.
p3: Closure 1872 → gains immediately reversed → educational and social progress lost without federal infrastructure to sustain it.

front: What was the impact of KKK terror during and after Reconstruction?
p1: KKK founded Tennessee 1865 → used violence to intimidate African Americans from voting, education, asserting rights.
p2: Colfax Massacre (1873) → c.100 African Americans killed in Louisiana following contested elections → federal government failed to help. New Orleans Massacre (1866): 40–200 killed.
p3: Enforcement Acts (1870–71) → Grant suppressed 1st KKK → over 600 prosecuted. But after 1877 troop withdrawal → KKK resurgent + unpunished.

front: What was the impact of lynching on African American social rights?
p1: Lynching epidemic → 100+ per year in early 1890s → used as tool of racial terror to enforce social hierarchy and deter political participation.
p2: Ida B. Wells → 'Southern Horrors' (1892) → documented frequency + disproved myth it was response to violent crime → national + international campaign.
p3: Southern Democratic politicians repeatedly defeated anti-lynching bills in Congress. In 1900, Governor Tillman of South Carolina openly defended lynching.

front: What was the impact of convict leasing on African Americans?
p1: Exploited 13th Amendment loophole → 'except as punishment for crime' → Southern states arrested African Americans on trivial charges → leased to private companies as unpaid labour.
p2: Grew across the South in the 1880s → effectively recreated slavery → dangerous conditions, no pay, no rights.
p3: System designed to control Black population + provide cheap labour to Southern economies → continued into early 20th century.

front: What was the role of anti-civil rights groups?
p1: KKK → violence at poll booths, lynching, destruction of Black organisations → Colfax Massacre (1873): 100+ killed to prevent voting.
p2: White Citizens Councils (1955) → 'respectable' opposition to integration → pressured employers, banks and landlords to discriminate → counterpart to KKK in the 1950s–60s.
p3: United Daughters of the Confederacy → 'Lost Cause' myth → romanticised slavery + Confederacy → justified Jim Crow → shaped Southern white opinion for generations.

front: What ideas and attitudes were used to justify Jim Crow?
p1: Lost Cause myth: United Daughters of the Confederacy romanticised slavery — Civil War as states' rights struggle → Confederate monuments, Birth of a Nation (1915) spread it nationally.
p2: Social Darwinism: framed African Americans as 'backward' on inferior civilisation rung → eugenic theories seen as modern science → justified racial separation.
p3: Religious: Richmond Times editor: 'God almighty drew the color line' → churches supported segregation → three pillars: Lost Cause (historical), Social Darwinism (scientific), religion (divine).

front: What was the significance of Birth of a Nation and the second KKK?
p1: Birth of a Nation (1915): D.W. Griffith film — glorified KKK, depicted Black men as violent sexual predators → screened at White House by Wilson who praised it → led directly to KKK revival.
p2: Second KKK: membership reached 5 million by 1920s — 15% of population → unlike first KKK, national not just Southern → included politicians, police chiefs, judges across North and West.
p3: 1925: Klan burned crosses outside NAACP offices → KKK members in public office undermined law enforcement → showed white supremacy was national not uniquely Southern.

front: What was the impact of WWI on African Americans?
p1: 380,000 African Americans served in segregated units → Harlem Hellfighters → stationed in Britain, experienced less segregated society → raised expectations. Wartime demand for labour → Great Migration accelerated
p2: NAACP membership grew as African Americans demanded rights in exchange for war service
p3: Red Summer (1919) → return of white soldiers + industrial retraction

front: What was the significance of the Harlem Renaissance?
p1: 1920s cultural explosion → Langston Hughes, Louis Armstrong, Zora Neale Hurston → Black artistic achievement gained national recognition.
p2: Harlem population grew 50,000 → 200,000 (1910–1930) → Du Bois used The Crisis to promote Black intellectualism → 100,000 circulation.
p3: Cultural flourishing did not translate into political or economic gains → KKK at 5 million same decade → Tulsa massacre (1921) destroyed 'Black Wall Street'.

front: What was the impact of the Tulsa Race Massacre (1921)?
p1: White mob destroyed Greenwood District ('Black Wall Street') → 600+ Black-owned businesses destroyed → 35 blocks burned.
p2: Up to 300 African Americans killed → 10,000 left homeless → one of worst incidents of racial violence in US history.
p3: Showed that Black economic success provoked violent white backlash → prosperity offered no protection without political and legal rights.

front: What was the impact of the Great Depression on African Americans?
p1: Black unemployment 50% vs 25% national average → 75% of Southern African Americans still sharecroppers → urban Black unemployment reached 20% in Chicago vs 12% white — before Depression.
p2: AFL had no affiliated Black unions → African Americans restricted to unprotected jobs → no Social Security for agricultural/domestic workers. NOI founded (1930)
p3: 50+ African Americans lynched annually in late 1920s → KKK 5 million members → social conditions deteriorated. BUT Great Depression shifted African Americans into Democratic coalition

front: What was the significance of the Double V Campaign and WWII service?
p1: NAACP launched Double V → victory against fascism abroad AND racism at home → exposed contradiction of fighting for democracy while denying it domestically.
p2: NAACP membership grew 50,000 → 500,000 during WWII → Cold War context made federal government increasingly conscious of international optics.
p3: Soviet propaganda publicised racial violence like Birmingham Campaign → Kennedy: 'We preach freedom around the world… but are we to say the land of the free — except for the negroes?'

front: What was the impact of the Emmett Till case (1955)?
p1: 14-year-old boy from Chicago murdered in Mississippi → body mutilated → murderers acquitted by all-white jury.
p2: Mother insisted on open-casket funeral → allowed media to share images of Emmett's body → spread outrage nationally and internationally.
p3: Galvanised civil rights movement → demonstrated that racial terror was ongoing + systemic → key catalyst for Montgomery Bus Boycott.

front: What was the role of Cold War context in advancing civil rights?
p1: Soviet propaganda publicised US racial violence to discredit America internationally → Birmingham Campaign broadcast globally.
p2: Federal Government increasingly conscious of Cold War optics → Kennedy: 'land of the free — except for the negroes?' after Birmingham.
p3: Decolonisation movements in 1950s–60s inspired African Americans → Gandhi + Kwame Nkrumah's actions influenced non-violent strategy.

front: What was the role of media in advancing the Civil Rights Movement?
p1: Televised images of Bloody Sunday (1965) + Birmingham Campaign (1963) shocked international audiences → generated massive support for movement.
p2: King adept at exploiting television cameras → chose Birmingham deliberately because Bull Connor guaranteed visible brutality → forced federal response.
p3: Emmett Till's open casket (1955) → media images of body spread outrage. Contrast with 19th century press → had perpetuated stereotypes + justified lynching.

front: What was the impact of the Vietnam War on the Civil Rights Movement?
p1: African Americans disproportionately drafted → returned radicalised + disillusioned → fed Black Power ethos of militancy.
p2: King's 'Beyond Vietnam' speech (1967) → severed relationship with LBJ → ended federal momentum on civil rights reforms.
p3: Media attention shifted from civil rights marches to anti-war protests → movement lost national spotlight → Black Power filled the vacuum.

front: What was the impact of the Black Panther Party's community programmes?
p1: Free breakfast programmes → fed 20,000 children per day → 'survival programmes' addressed poverty the civil rights legislation had not solved.
p2: 13 health clinics established → screened thousands for sickle cell anaemia → People's Free Medical Centres in 13 deprived areas. 60+ community schools.
p3: BPP's 10-Point Programme demanded reparations, land, full employment, decent housing → shifted civil rights agenda from legal equality to economic justice.

front: What were the Long Hot Summers (1967) and what caused them?
p1: 150 race riots in 1967 → largest in Detroit and Newark → response to poverty, police brutality and de facto segregation in Northern cities.
p2: Watts (1965) $40m property damage → exposed failure of non-violence + civil rights legislation to address systemic Northern inequality.
p3: Showed CRM had not resolved economic grievances → MLK's assassination (1968) triggered new wave of riots → Nixon won on 'Law and Order' ticket.

front: What was the impact of COINTELPRO on Black Power organisations?
p1: FBI infiltrated Black Power groups → planted informants → manufactured evidence → created internal suspicion + divisions.
p2: Arrests + assassinations: Fred Hampton (Black Panther leader) killed in FBI-orchestrated raid 1969 → Panthers collapsed by 1982.
p3: Panthers never exceeded 5,000 members → COINTELPRO accelerated collapse → demonstrated state willingness to use illegal tactics against civil rights organisations.

front: What was the significance of the Los Angeles Riots (1992)?
p1: Erupted after acquittal of LAPD officers for beating Rodney King by all-white jury → $1 billion of damage → 63 killed.
p2: Demonstrated that police brutality + racial injustice remained systemic → civil rights legislation had not changed ground realities for urban Black communities.
p3: Positive strides by 1992 → Oprah, Michael Jordan, Spike Lee as icons of Black success → but persistent stereotypes + poverty for majority remained.

front: Why did sharecropping trap African Americans in poverty?
p1: No land redistribution → '40 acres and a mule' never realised → freedpeople forced to farm same land, same landowner as during slavery.
p2: Crop-lien system → sharecroppers paid rent in crops → always in debt to landowner → could not leave without repaying debt → effective debt bondage.
p3: By 1900 only 25% of African Americans owned land → economic freedom impossible without land ownership → Southern economic system rebuilt on near-slavery.

front: What evidence is there of Black economic success during the Gilded Age?
p1: Tuskegee Institute (1881): Washington trained artisans and professionals → by 1900: 50,000 Black professionals — doctors, lawyers, teachers → African Americans owned 15 million acres of land by early 1900s
p2: Parallel economy: barbershops, undertakers, small shops formed basis of Black middle class → Greenwood District, Tulsa ('Black Wall Street'): 600+ businesses → Harlem: population 50,000 → 200,000 (1910-30)
p3: Du Bois: first Black Harvard PhD (1895) → NAACP founded 1909 → Great Migration (1916-70): 6 million moved North

front: What was the significance of the Great Migration?
p1: 1916–1970 → over 6 million African Americans moved from rural South to Northern + Western cities → escaping Jim Crow + seeking economic opportunity.
p2: Created influential Black urban communities → Harlem + South Side Chicago → fostered cultural and political movements → WWI phase: 500,000 moved 1916–19.
p3: Opened skilled industrial jobs in North → 40% of Black men in North held skilled jobs by 1920 vs 15% in South → but de facto segregation + racial hostility persisted.

front: How did the First New Deal affect African Americans economically?
p1: FERA → direct relief → 20–30% of recipients were African American. CCC → employed c.200,000 African Americans (10% of enrolment). PWA → 65,000+ in infrastructure jobs by 1940.
p2: Some Black sharecroppers became independent farmers through federal assistance → Black Cabinet influenced programme delivery.
p3: AAA (1933) inadvertently displaced 200,000 Black sharecroppers → NRA codes manipulated by employers → gains were partial and unevenly distributed.

front: How did the Second New Deal affect African Americans?
p1: WPA → infrastructure jobs → 15% of workers were African American. Social Security Act → pensions + unemployment insurance for the first time.
p2: Wagner Act (1935) → recognised BSCP → first Black union to win AFL recognition → but inadvertently created 'closed shops' → white-only unions could dominate.
p3: Bethune's role in NYA → funded training + jobs for 600,000 Black youths during Depression → most direct targeted benefit for African Americans.

front: What were the economic limitations of the New Deal for African Americans?
p1: Social Security excluded agricultural + domestic workers → 65% of Black workers → most significant exclusion from New Deal economic protection.
p2: Aid administered by Southern states → whites controlled distribution → African Americans discriminated against in application of relief policies.
p3: Anti-Communist Red Scare → organisations advocating for Black economic rights suspected of communism → CIO lost funding → unions weakened.

front: What was the impact of Executive Order 8802 (1941)?
p1: Randolph's March on Washington Movement threatened 100,000-strong march → pressured FDR → EO 8802 banned racial discrimination in defence industries.
p2: By end of WWII → 2 million+ African Americans employed in defence industries → significant wartime economic opportunity.
p3: First time a mass non-violent movement forced a major federal economic concession → model for later civil rights pressure tactics.

front: What were the post-war economic challenges facing African Americans?
p1: GI Bill (1944): provided education, housing loans and job training to veterans — but administered locally in the South
p2: Automation: post-WWII manufacturing shift disproportionately hit African Americans concentrated in low-skill manual jobs. Black unemployment double white unemployment. Manufacturing jobs eliminated were precisely those gained during Great Migration and wartime production.
p3: Continued violence: NAACP recorded 56 Black veterans attacked, some in uniform, in 1919. Pattern repeated post-WWII — returning veterans who asserted rights targeted. Economic exclusion compounded by residential segregation in the North and West.

front: What was the impact of the Great Society on African Americans?
p1: Medicare + Medicaid (1965) → Black Americans with health insurance: 25% → 75% by 1970. Food Stamp Act (1964) → 33% of recipients were African American despite being 12% of population.
p2: Civil Rights Act (1964) → prohibited employment discrimination → EEOC enforcement → African Americans in white-collar jobs: 5% (1960) → 15% (mid-1970s).
p3: Despite legislation → by 1970 Black families earned average 58% of white families → CRM failed to make economic gains in Northern cities.

front: What was the impact of affirmative action on African Americans?
p1: First introduced Philadelphia 1969 → spread nationally → African Americans in white-collar jobs: 5% (1960) → 15% (mid-1970s) → growing Black middle class.
p2: Regents of University of California v Bakke (1978) → racial quotas unconstitutional → weakened programme. Reagan/Bush labelled it 'reverse discrimination' → federal enforcement reduced.
p3: By 1980s → 40% of African Americans middle class → but gains uneven → 'bifurcation' → persistent ghetto poverty alongside professional success.

front: What was the economic position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: African Americans earned 60% of average white income → Black unemployment 14.2% vs 7.2% white → overrepresented in low-wage sectors.
p2: Homeownership 43% vs 70% white → redlining + discriminatory lending had lasting effects → urban renewal projects displaced many Black communities.
p3: 500,000+ Black-owned businesses → $10 billion gross revenue → 40% middle class → but 33% below poverty line → 'bifurcation' defined economic reality by 1992.

front: How different were AA experiences outside the South in the Gilded Age?
p1: North → better industrial jobs + education → growing Black middle class → BUT de facto segregation — Chicago 5,000 confined to one area; NY Harlem separate district for 23,000
p2: West → relative racial indifference → cowboys, trappers, miners, shopkeepers → Bass Reeves: Deputy US Marshal, arrested thousands → Mary Fields: famous stagecoach driver
p3: Limits → Exoduster movement (1879): 40,000 fled South to Kansas → faced hostility + hardship → racial violence still present

front: What were the key Supreme Court cases during the Gilded Age?
p1: States' Rights doctrine → Supreme Court ruled 14th Amendment only protected national citizenship → states free to discriminate → gave constitutional backing to white supremacy throughout the Gilded Age
p2: Plessy v Ferguson (1896) → 'separate but equal' constitutional → Jim Crow legal cover for 58 years
p3: Mississippi v Williams (1898) → upheld literacy tests + poll taxes → by 1900, 90% of Southern African Americans disenfranchised → Supreme Court = instrument of oppression, not protection

front: What was the significance of W.E.B. Du Bois?
p1: First Black Harvard PhD (1895) → Niagara Movement (1905): demanded full civil + political rights, directly opposed Washington → co-founded NAACP (1909) → The Crisis: 100,000 subscribers by 1920
p2: 'Talented tenth' → educated Black professional class to lead liberation through intellect + political agitation → Pan-Africanism: organised Pan-African Congresses 1919, 1921, 1923 → linked AA struggle to global anti-colonialism
p3: Limits → middle-class focus → struggled to connect with poorest African Americans → socialist leanings → FBI surveillance during Red Scare → emigrated to Ghana 1961, disillusioned with American racism

front: How strong was the position of African Americans by 1932?
p1: Progress: literacy 10% (1865) → 85% (1930) → 300,000 in Northern schools → NAACP won US v Guinn (1915) removing grandfather clauses → Great Migration created Harlem Renaissance
p2: Weakness: only 2% registered to vote in South → 75% still sharecroppers → Black unemployment 50% vs 25% national (Depression) → KKK 15% of eligible population
p3: Structural limits: anti-lynching bills repeatedly blocked → Reconstruction gains fully reversed in South → NAACP legal successes but no political power

front: Was Roosevelt's administration an effective supporter of African American rights?
p1: Effective: appointed more Black Americans to gov than any predecessor → Black Cabinet led by Bethune → Eleanor Roosevelt resigned DAR to support Marian Anderson (1939)
p2: Political shift: ¾ AA voted Republican 1932 → ¾ voted Democrat 1936 → fundamental realignment → WPA employed 1 million+ AA by 1939 → Harold Ickes pushed anti-segregation policies
p3: Ineffective: refused anti-lynching bill — feared losing Southern Democrats → AAA displaced 200,000 Black sharecroppers → Social Security excluded 65% of Black workers → CCC segregated

front: What was the cultural impact of Black Power?
p1: Black Arts Movement (1965–75): Amiri Baraka founded Black Arts Repertory Theatre 1965 — 'cultural wing of Black Power' → 500+ Black arts organisations
p2: 500+ Black Studies programmes in US universities by 1971 → demanded by student activists → Afro hairstyle, dashikis = acts of political assertion
p3: Limits → cultural gains did not translate to economic/political progress → mainly felt by middle-class + educated → those in ghettos saw little change

front: What was the role of State Governments in hindering AA rights?
p1: Black Codes (1865–6) → restricted movement, labour and assembly of freedmen → de facto re-enslavement before federal repeal
p2: Voter suppression: Mississippi (1890) → literacy tests, poll taxes, grandfather clauses → Black voter registration: 90% (1867) → 6% (1892) → spread across South
p3: State govts took no action on racial violence → Governor Tillman SC openly defended lynching (1900) → 1,875 lynchings in 1890s alone

front: What was the position of labour and union rights in 1865?
p1: No legal protections for unions — courts upheld employers' right to suppress organising. 20 state governments had laws allowing militias to intervene in labour disputes
p2: NLU (1866): 300,000 members at peak — but collapsed after Sylvis's death (1869). Craft unions like Cigar Makers represented less than 10% of workers in any industry
p3: Working conditions dire: 3,000 railroad workers killed and 20,000 injured annually in early 1870s. 750,000 children under 15 in industrial labour. Immigrants worked 60–70 hours/week for as little as $1/day

front: What was the significance of the Great Railroad Strike (1877)?
p1: Spontaneous nationwide strike following wage cuts during economic depression — spread from West Virginia across the country. Workers from different railroads shut down rail traffic.
p2: Federal troops called in — killed over 100 workers. Government's focus on maintaining order rather than addressing workers' grievances.
p3: First nationwide labour dispute → exposed need for stronger organised unions → showed federal violent resistance was the government's default response to strikes.

front: What was the significance of the NLU, CNLU and KOL?
p1: NLU (1866): first national labour organisation — Sylvis pushed for 8-hour workday and legislative reforms. Undermined by economic depression of early 1870s and internal divisions — over-reliant on Sylvis, collapsed 1869.
p2: CNLU (1869): formed by African American workers excluded from NLU — showed racial divisions embedded from the start. KOL (1869): most inclusive early union — welcomed skilled and unskilled, women, African Americans and immigrants.
p3: Molly Maguires (1873): violent conflicts in Pennsylvania coalfields — Pinkerton agents infiltrated, 10 leaders executed 1876. Associated unions with violence — damaged public support.

front: What was the significance of the Haymarket Affair (1886)?
p1: KOL grew from 20,000 (1881) to 700,000 (1886) — most inclusive labour organisation, welcomed women, African Americans and immigrants. Rally in Chicago demanding 8-hour workday turned violent — bomb killed 7 police officers.
p2: KOL collapsed — associated with radicalism and anarchism. AFL (1886) established as safer alternative under Gompers — focused on skilled workers only, excluded unskilled, women and most African Americans.
p3: Haymarket associated industrial unionism with anarchism in public mind — damaged union movement for decades. Showed employer and government hostility could destroy even a 700,000-strong organisation.

front: What was the significance of the Homestead Strike (1892)?
p1: Carnegie Steel locked out Amalgamated Association workers — wage cuts + anti-union. 300 Pinkerton agents arrived by barge, 12 dead in violent clash. 8,000 state militia deployed — workers defeated.
p2: AFL refused to support — exposed skilled/unskilled division. Steel industry union-free until 1930s. Homestead virtually bankrupted the union. Carnegie's absence in Scotland damaged his 'workers' friend' reputation.
p3: Showed corporations would use private armies and state force against workers. Highlighted Gilded Age employer power. Contrast: Flint sit-down (1936–37) finally won UAW recognition — over 40 years later.

front: What was the role of the AFL during the Gilded Age?
p1: Founded 1886 by Samuel Gompers — focused on skilled workers, pushed for higher wages, shorter workdays and better conditions through collective bargaining rather than confrontation
p2: Exclusionary by design — neglected unskilled labourers, women and most African Americans
p3: Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) routinely used against unions as illegal restraints of trade

front: What was the significance of the Great Coal Strike (1902)?
p1: 140,000 miners — demanded higher wages, shorter hours and union recognition. President Roosevelt intervened to arbitrate rather than send troops — first time federal government acted as mediator not suppressor.
p2: Mitchell's moderate UMWA leadership secured presidential support — Roosevelt more sympathetic to Mitchell than the abrasive company owners. Owners agreed to wage increase and improved conditions.
p3: Partial success — marked shift in Progressive Era attitude. BUT no formal union recognition. Showed moderate leadership could achieve more than confrontation. First positive federal intervention in a labour dispute.

front: What was the significance of the IWW and Lawrence Textile Strike?
p1: IWW ('Wobblies') founded 1905 — sought to unite all workers regardless of skill, including immigrants and minorities. Open to groups excluded by AFL
p2: Lawrence Textile 'Bread and Roses' Strike (1912): immigrant women from multiple ethnic groups — IWW-led. Women received 15% pay rise and overtime pay
p3: Showed power of solidarity across ethnic lines. BUT IWW's radical tactics ultimately led to its suppression — radical methods alienated moderates

front: What was the impact of WWI and the Red Scare on labour?
p1: NWLB (1918): agreement between employers and AFL to maintain production — temporarily legitimised unions and facilitated collective bargaining. BUT policies only benefited AFL — excluded unskilled and unaffiliated workers.
p2: AFL agreed no-strike pledges during WWI — prioritised national unity. Seattle General Strike (1919): 65,000 workers — suppressed by Mayor Hanson, demonised by media as Bolshevist
p3: Red Summer (1919): race riots across major US cities — economic tensions between Black and white workers competing for jobs. Post-war reversal — all wartime gains quickly rolled back

front: What was the impact of welfare capitalism in the 1920s?
p1: Employers introduced pensions, healthcare and benefits — reduced perceived need for unions. Yellow-dog contracts widespread — workers signed away right to join unions as condition of employment
p2: Union membership declined from peak of 5 million (1920). Deering v Duplex (1921): restricted secondary boycotts
p3: BSCP founded 1925 by Philip Randolph — first successful Black union, sought recognition from Pullman Company and AFL. Would not achieve it until 1937

front: What was the significance of the Wagner Act (1935)?
p1: Guaranteed right to unionise and collectively bargain — established NLRB to enforce. Banned company spies, company unions, blacklisting and dismissal of union organisers. Union membership: 3 million (1933)
p2: Wagner Act promoted closed shops — but this inadvertently excluded Black workers from AFL unions. Social Security (1935) excluded farm and domestic workers — 65% of Black workers
p3: Milestone in labour rights — first time federal government legally recognised workers' right to organise. BUT relied on Southern Democrats who used local administration to undermine it

front: What was the significance of the CIO and Flint Sit-Down Strike?
p1: John Lewis formed CIO (1935) as part of AFL — focused on industrial workers regardless of skill, including women and African Americans
p2: Flint Sit-Down Strike (1936–37): 40,000 workers at General Motors — CIO-led. Workers occupied the factory rather than picketing outside — harder to replace. Forced recognition of UAW
p3: US Steel unionised 1937 without a strike — over 40 years after Homestead failure. NLRB v Fansteel (1939): sit-down strikes ruled illegal

front: What was the significance of Philip Randolph and the BSCP?
p1: BSCP founded 1925 — first successful Black union. Randolph became first African American to lead a national union that won a collective bargaining agreement
p2: March on Washington Movement (1941): threatened 100,000-strong march on Washington — pressured Roosevelt to issue EO 8802, prohibiting racial discrimination in defence industries
p3: Significance beyond labour: demonstrated power of non-violent mass pressure — model later used by civil rights movement. BSCP's success relied on shift in federal attitudes with New Deal

front: What was the impact of the Taft-Hartley Act (1947)?
p1: Passed over Truman's veto — amended Wagner Act. Banned secondary strikes and closed shops
p2: Required union leaders to sign anti-communist oaths — fostered division within movement, weakened CIO whose leaders included communists
p3: Post-WWII strike wave (1946): 5,000 strikes involving 4.6 million workers — showed pent-up pressure. Taft-Hartley imposed 60-day cooling-off period for strikes threatening national security

front: What was the significance of the AFL-CIO merger (1955)?
p1: AFL and CIO merged — 16 million members, representing 85% of unionised workforce. Combined both craft and industrial unions into one huge negotiating bloc
p2: Automation 1950s–60s: manufacturing job losses — blue-collar unions weakened. New white-collar workers uninterested in labour struggle. New electronics and service sectors relocated to avoid unions
p3: OSHA (1970): established workplace safety standards — significantly reduced workplace injuries and deaths. Civil Rights Act (1964): prohibited employment discrimination by race, sex or national origin

front: What was the significance of Cesar Chavez and the UFW?
p1: UFW (1966): Chavez organised Filipino and Mexican American farm workers — historically without union representation, excluded from most labour legislation
p2: Salad Bowl Strike (1970): led by Filipino workers, supported by Mexican and other ethnic groups. Success — strengthened UFW's position, led to better wages and union recognition for farm workers
p3: Showed power of nonviolent strikes and consumer boycotts beyond the workplace. Expanded labour movement beyond its traditional white male industrial base — major increase in Hispanic union membership

front: What was the significance of DRUM and the LRBW?
p1: DRUM (Dodge Revolutionary Union Movement, 1968): established in Detroit → organised wildcat strikes in Dodge auto plants → demanded racial equality for Black workers in UAW.
p2: LRBW (League of Revolutionary Black Workers): umbrella organisation → pushed for Black leadership in UAW → Black workers 30% of UAW membership by early 1970s but underrepresented in leadership → earned $2,000 less annually.
p3: Limits: UAW leadership resistant despite similar tactics having founded CIO in 1930s → LRBW collapsed by mid-1970s due to internal divisions and FBI COINTELPRO surveillance.

front: What was the impact of the PATCO Strike (1981)?
p1: Air traffic controllers struck for $10,000 pay rise, improved conditions and reduced hours. Reagan declared strike illegal — fired 11,000 workers and banned them from federal employment. Effectively decertified the union.
p2: Marked decisive shift in balance of power between government and unions — emboldened employers across all industries to adopt anti-union stances. Union-busting became standard practice. Outsourcing and non-unionised temporary workers normalised.
p3: PATCO alienated public — seen as demanding excessive pay rise during summer holidays, making Reagan's response politically easy. Union membership: 24% (1979)

front: What was the position of labour and union rights by 1992?
p1: Union membership 16% of workforce — down from 35% (1945) and 24% (1979). Deindustrialisation, automation and globalisation eroded traditional union base. Manufacturing jobs declined 40% from 1970 peak.
p2: Legal framework survived: Wagner Act, NLRB, OSHA, Civil Rights Act (1964), Equal Pay Act (1963) all in force. But employers routinely used union-busting consultants and relocated to right-to-work states
p3: AFL-CIO members still earned more than non-unionised workers but gap narrowing. Women and minority workers still disproportionately in non-unionised, lower-paid roles

front: What were working conditions like during the Gilded Age?
p1: 2,000 rail workers killed in accidents in 1889 alone → by 1900: 35,000 workplace deaths annually → no federal safety legislation → no compensation for injury or death
p2: Women: 15% of industrial workforce → earned $3-6/week vs $7-10 for men → immigrants: 15-20% of urban industrial workforce → worked 10-12 hours/day, 6 days/week
p3: 2% of population owned 30% of wealth → no legal framework for workers' rights → no minimum wage, no safety standards, no union recognition

front: What was the significance of Eugene Debs and the ARU?
p1: ARU (1894): first successful industrial union — mobilised railroad workers across industries regardless of skill. Debs led Pullman Strike (1894) — although defeated, brought national attention to plight of workers.
p2: Debs' advocacy for socialism led him to run for president multiple times as Socialist Party candidate — won 6% of vote in 1912
p3: ARU showed potential of industrial unionism — organising workers across all industries within a sector. BUT AFL refused to support ARU during Pullman strike — skilled/unskilled division fatally weakened it

front: What was the role of divisions in the Gilded Age labour movement?
p1: Skilled vs unskilled: AFL excluded unskilled workers → Pullman (1894) failed partly because AFL refused to support ARU → Homestead (1892): AFL refused to support Amalgamated Association → steel union-free until 1930s.
p2: Racial: NLU excluded Black workers → CNLU formed separately (1869) → African Americans used as strike-breakers → fewer than 5% of AFL members Black → Red Summer (1919) partly driven by job competition.
p3: Immigration: 11 million new immigrants → race to bottom on wages → AFL promoted immigration restrictions → employers deliberately exploited ethnic divisions to prevent solidarity.

front: How did the courts shape labour rights in the Progressive Era?
p1: Lochner v New York (1905): Supreme Court struck down law limiting bakers' hours — 'freedom of contract' → blocked state worker protections → set precedent used to block safety legislation.
p2: Clayton Antitrust Act (1914): attempted to exempt unions from antitrust → Duplex v Deering (1921) limited it → Keating-Owen Child Labour Act (1916): struck down by Hammer v Dagenhart (1918).
p3: Norris-LaGuardia Act (1932): finally banned yellow-dog contracts → Wagner Act (1935) transformed landscape → courts had obstructed labour rights for 30 years before New Deal broke through.

front: What was the significance of the Seattle General Strike (1919)?
p1: 65,000 workers across various industries struck in solidarity — largest general strike in US history to that point. Aimed to show power of cross-industry solidarity beyond a single workplace dispute.
p2: Suppressed by Mayor Ole Hanson — described as a Bolshevist revolution. Media demonised strikers as anarchists and communists
p3: Red Scare (1919): Bolshevik Revolution in Russia sparked fears of global communist revolution — union activity viewed with deep suspicion. All post-WWI labour gains rapidly reversed

front: What was the impact of the Great Depression on labour rights?
p1: Wall St Crash (1929)
p2: Norris-LaGuardia Act (1932): prohibited federal courts from using injunctions against peaceful strikes and banned yellow-dog contracts — first significant legislative gain in decades. Unions had only 3 million members by 1932 — a fraction of the workforce.
p3: Great Depression created conditions for New Deal — showed welfare capitalism had failed. Workers' desperation drove Flint sit-down strikes and pressure for Wagner Act. In 1932, ¾ of African Americans still voted Republican — political realignment not yet complete.

front: What was the significance of the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938)?
p1: $25 weekly minimum wage established — first federal minimum wage. Maximum working hours legislated. Child labour under 16 banned in industries engaged in interstate commerce.
p2: Passed despite opposition from business groups — showed New Deal coalition could overcome employer resistance
p3: Limits: did not address gender pay gap — women still earned significantly less than men. Excluded farm and domestic workers — sectors with large proportion of Black and immigrant workers

front: What was the impact of McCarthyism on the labour movement?
p1: McCarthyism (1947-57): anti-communist hysteria → Taft-Hartley (1947) required union leaders to sign anti-communist oaths → leaders who refused lost NLRB access.
p2: CIO expelled 11 radical unions (1949-50) — those most inclusive of Black workers and women → weakened labour's most progressive wing → AFL-CIO merger (1955) under moderate leadership.
p3: FBI COINTELPRO targeted radical union organisers → Du Bois surveilled → labour-left alliance fractured → unions became more conservative → membership peaked 35% (1945) → began slow decline.

front: What was the impact of automation and deindustrialisation?
p1: Automation (1950s-70s): manufacturing jobs declining → blue-collar unions weakened as workforce shifted to service sector → new electronics and service sectors relocated to avoid unions.
p2: Deindustrialisation: by 1979 manufacturing jobs had declined 40% from 1970 peak → union strongholds in steel, auto and rubber collapsed → Rust Belt poverty.
p3: Reagan era: union-busting consultants, outsourcing, relocation to right-to-work states → PATCO (1981): 11,000 workers fired → union membership: 35% (1945) → 16% (1992).

front: What was the impact of gender and racial divisions post-war?
p1: Post-war: women pushed out of unionised jobs as men returned → AFL-CIO leadership predominantly male → Taft-Hartley (1947) weakened unions most inclusive of minorities.
p2: Racial: AFL-CIO marginalised Black workers → McCarthyism forced CIO to expel radical (most inclusive) unions → Black workers earned $2,000 less annually than white equivalents.
p3: Equal Pay Act (1963): first federal legislation on pay discrimination → Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: prohibited employment discrimination by sex and race.

front: What was the impact of Reaganomics on labour rights?
p1: Deregulation and tax cuts for business — union-busting became standard practice. Employers used legal challenges, outsourcing and non-unionised temporary workers to weaken unions. Relocating to right-to-work states normalised.
p2: Reagan reduced OSHA funding — workplace safety declined, safety violations persisted especially in agriculture and construction. Judicial appointments shifted courts in a more employer-friendly direction — weakened NLRB enforcement.
p3: Union membership: 24% (1979)

front: What was the position of labour rights in 1865?
p1: No legal protections: no minimum wage, no safety standards, no union recognition → 2,000 rail workers killed in 1889 alone → children worked 12-hour shifts → unskilled workers earned $1-3/week.
p2: Unions in infancy: NLU (1866) — collapsed after leader Sylvis died (1869) → KOL (1869): 20,000 members growing → no federal labour legislation → workers entirely at employer mercy.
p3: Wages: women earned half male wages → immigrants accepted lower → Black workers excluded from most unions → CNLU (1869) formed separately → fewer than 5% of workers unionised.

front: What was the impact of the Panic of 1873 on labour?
p1: Panic of 1873: railroad overexpansion → financial collapse → 25% unemployment in some cities → wages halved → Great Railroad Strike (1877): spontaneous walkout, 100+ killed by federal troops.
p2: NLU collapsed 1873 → KOL grew in response — 700,000 by 1886 → National Guard deployed 23 times in 1892 alone → employers used Depression to cut wages and break unions.
p3: Coxey's Army (1894): 500 unemployed marched on Washington demanding federal relief → arrested for walking on grass.

front: What was the role of racial and ethnic divisions in early labour?
p1: Chinese Exclusion Act (1882): AFL supported → nativist hostility within labour movement → Foran Act (1885): banned contract labour from Europe.
p2: CNLU (1869): Black workers formed national union after exclusion from NLU → AFL refused to admit Black workers → race riots during strikes — employers hired Black workers as strike-breakers.
p3: Employers deliberately exploited race and ethnicity to prevent solidarity → unions split along ethnic lines throughout Gilded Age.

front: How significant was opposition to New Deal labour reforms?
p1: Employer resistance: many employers resisted Wagner Act through blacklisting, spy networks and private security → Henry Ford: Battle of the Overpass (1937) — Ford thugs beat UAW organisers
p2: Internal divisions: AFL-CIO split (1938) — AFL expelled CIO → exposed fractures → AFL promoted closed shops that inadvertently excluded Black workers
p3: Limits of opposition: union membership surged 3.7 million (1933) → 9 million (1938) despite resistance → US Steel unionised 1937 without strike → Ford finally recognised UAW 1941

front: What was the significance of the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire (1911)?
p1: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory, New York, March 1911 → fire broke out → owners had locked exit doors → 146 garment workers killed — mostly young Italian and Jewish immigrant women.
p2: 100,000 marched at victims' funeral → New York Factory Commission led by Frances Perkins → 36 new labour laws enacted: fire safety, working hours, machine guards, sanitation.
p3: Perkins later used findings to shape New Deal legislation → showed male union neglect had lethal consequences → WTUL used tragedy to build pressure for state-level reform.

front: What was the significance of the Clayton Antitrust Act (1914)?
p1: Clayton Antitrust Act (1914): attempted to exempt unions from antitrust laws → prevented courts using Sherman Act to issue injunctions against strikes → Gompers called it 'labour's Magna Carta'.
p2: Impact limited: Duplex v Deering (1921) — Supreme Court upheld injunctions against secondary boycotts → courts continued to issue injunctions restricting strikes throughout 1920s.
p3: Norris-LaGuardia Act (1932): finally prohibited federal courts from issuing injunctions against peaceful strikes → effectively delivered what Clayton Act had promised but failed to achieve.

front: What was the significance of the Women's Trade Union League (1903)?
p1: Coalition of working-class women and middle-class reformers — advocated for better wages, shorter hours and unionisation for women workers
p2: Exposed the exclusion of women from male-dominated unions like the AFL
p3: Limitations: AFL remained hostile to women's full membership. Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911) exposed inadequacy of existing protections

front: What was the NIRA/NRA (1933) and why did it fail?
p1: NIRA (1933): codes protecting workers — minimum wages, maximum hours, child labour bans → Section 7a: workers' right to organise → 'Blue Eagle' symbol for compliant firms.
p2: Declared unconstitutional 1935 (Schechter Poultry v US): exceeded federal power → many employers had displayed Blue Eagle while ignoring codes.
p3: NIRA's failure proved voluntary codes insufficient → directly led to Wagner Act (1935) with real NLRB enforcement → NIRA failure was catalyst for New Deal's most important labour reform.

front: What was employer and state resistance to New Deal labour reforms?
p1: Employer resistance: many continued blacklisting and spy networks despite NLRB → Henry Ford: Battle of the Overpass (1937) — thugs beat UAW organisers
p2: Memorial Day Massacre (1937): Chicago police killed 10 striking steelworkers at Republic Steel → employers used local and state police as private armies
p3: BUT: Ford finally recognised UAW 1941 → US Steel unionised 1937 → union membership 3.7 million (1933) → 9 million (1938)

front: What was the significance of NLRB v Fansteel and Ford UAW (1941)?
p1: NLRB v Fansteel (1939): Supreme Court ruled sit-down strikes were illegal → undermined key CIO tactic that had won GM recognition at Flint
p2: Ford recognition (1941): Henry Ford — last major industrial employer to accept union power → recognised UAW after NLRB elections showed overwhelming majority support → ended 20-year battle
p3: Together: sit-down strikes outlawed BUT NLRB elections proved effective → showed New Deal framework could deliver union recognition even without most militant tactics

front: What was the post-WWII strike wave (1946) and its consequences?
p1: 1946: 5,000 strikes, 4.6 million workers — largest strike wave in U.S. history → pent-up pressure from wartime no-strike pledges → steel, auto, coal, railways all struck.
p2: Public backlash: disruption of essential services eroded sympathy → Republicans won Congress in 1946 mid-terms partly on anti-union platform.
p3: Taft-Hartley (1947): passed over Truman's veto → banned secondary strikes and closed shops → allowed right-to-work laws → required anti-communist oaths from union leaders.

front: What was the significance of Landrum-Griffin and Kennedy EO 10988?
p1: Landrum-Griffin Act (1959): increased federal oversight of union internal affairs → required regular elections, financial reporting → reduced corruption but curtailed political activities and picketing.
p2: Kennedy EO 10988 (1962): granted federal employees right to organise — but not to strike → OSHA (1970): first comprehensive federal workplace safety law → Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: prohibited employment discrimination.
p3: AFL-CIO members earned 20% more than non-unionised workers by 1960s → BUT automation threatened: manufacturing jobs declining → white-collar workers uninterested in unions.

front: What was the impact of the Equal Pay Act and CRA on labour?
p1: Equal Pay Act (1963): first federal law prohibiting pay discrimination by sex → women earning 59 cents per dollar → by 1973: 71 cents → enforcement limited.
p2: Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: prohibited employment discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex and national origin → EEOC established to enforce → NOW (1966) formed partly to pressure EEOC.
p3: BUT: glass ceiling persisted → gender and racial pay gaps narrowed slowly → women and Black workers underrepresented in management throughout.

front: What was the significance of OSHA (1970)?
p1: OSHA (1970): first comprehensive federal workplace safety law → established minimum safety standards across all industries → required employers to report workplace injuries and deaths.
p2: Impact: workplace fatalities fell from over 14,000 annually in 1930s to approximately 4,500 by 1990s → significant reduction in workplace injuries and occupational diseases.
p3: Limits: Reagan reduced OSHA funding → safety violations persisted especially in agriculture and construction → agricultural workers excluded from key provisions.

front: What was the significance of Red Cloud's War and Fort Laramie?
p1: Red Cloud's War (1866-68): Lakota Sioux defeated U.S. Army in Powder River Country → Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868): guaranteed Black Hills 'in perpetuity'.
p2: Gold discovered (1874): government demanded sale → Sioux refused → 1877: Black Hills seized in violation of treaty → government threatened to stop rations.
p3: Little Bighorn (1876): Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull annihilated Custer's 7th Cavalry → only major Native military victory → BUT federal response intensified → Wounded Knee (1890) followed.

front: What was the impact of the Civil War and westward expansion on Natives?
p1: Civil War (1861-65): Sand Creek Massacre (1864) — militia killed 150+ peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho → some tribes (Cherokee) allied with Confederacy → 30,000 troops stationed across West by 1870.
p2: Homestead Act (1862): 160-acre plots to settlers → encroached on Native lands → Transcontinental railroad (1869): opened West → railway companies given land taken from tribes.
p3: Buffalo: 30 million (1860) → less than 1,000 (1889) → deliberate extermination → Plains tribes lost economic independence → forced onto reservations.

front: What was the significance of the Battle of Little Bighorn (1876)?
p1: Little Bighorn (1876): Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull led 2,000+ warriors → annihilated Custer's 7th Cavalry — 268 soldiers killed → only major Native military victory of the Plains Wars.
p2: Federal response intensified: Army flooded Plains → Sitting Bull fled to Canada → Crazy Horse surrendered 1877, killed at Fort Robinson → Black Hills seized → Wounded Knee (1890).
p3: Military resistance could achieve tactical victories → BUT federal resources ultimately overwhelming → Little Bighorn accelerated dispossession rather than preventing it.

front: What was the impact of the Homestead Act and railroad on Natives?
p1: Homestead Act (1862): granted settlers 160-acre plots → directly encroached on Native lands → Transcontinental railroad completed (1869): opened West to settlers, miners and cattle ranchers.
p2: Government granted railway companies 170 million acres — much taken from tribes → railroad destroyed buffalo migration patterns → enabled hunters to penetrate deep into Plains.
p3: Indian Appropriations Act (1871): ended treaty-making → tribes no longer independent nations — 'wards of the state' → Dawes Act (1887) broke up even reservation land into individual allotments.

front: What was the Dawes Severalty Act (1887) and how did it work?
p1: Dawes Act (1887): divided communal tribal lands → 160-acre allotments (320 for grazing) per male head of family
p2: Native land: 156 million acres (1881) → 78 million acres by 1890 → 90 million acres lost in under 50 years → Curtis Act (1898): extended to Five Civilised Tribes
p3: Wheeler-Howard Act (1934): halted allotment → restored only 4 million of 90 million acres lost → by 1932 two-thirds of Native land lost since Dawes Act

front: What was the cultural and gendered impact of the Dawes Act?
p1: Imposed male-headed family ownership onto matriarchal tribes → Iroquois and Cherokee women traditionally managed land → Dawes Act stripped this role
p2: Allotment scattered families across individual plots → broke up spatial concentration of tribes → undermined communal ceremonies, governance and economic co-operation
p3: Land sold to speculators: most allotted land poor quality → arid, infertile, unsuitable for farming → most sold allotments → left destitute

front: What was the impact of the Curtis Act and sovereignty court cases?
p1: Curtis Act (1898): extended Dawes Act to Five Civilised Tribes → destroyed governments of Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek and Seminole → ended their legal self-governance → allotment imposed without consent.
p2: Crow Dog Case (1883): Supreme Court recognised tribal criminal jurisdiction → BUT this prompted Major Crimes Act (1885): federal jurisdiction over 7 serious crimes on reservations
p3: Lone Wolf v Hitchcock (1903): Congress could unilaterally revoke treaties → cemented federal control → combined with Indian Appropriations Act (1871) and Curtis Act: complete destruction of tribal legal standing.

front: What was the Ghost Dance Movement (1889) and what did it represent?
p1: Ghost Dance Movement (1889): founded by Wovoka (Paiute prophet) → combined traditional beliefs with hope of driving away white settlers and restoring Native lands
p2: Federal government alarmed: mass gatherings seen as military threat → Sitting Bull arrested and killed by Indian police (December 1890) → 7th Cavalry surrounded Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek
p3: Significance: end of armed Plains Indian resistance → Ghost Dance suppressed — last major cultural resistance movement of the period → Wounded Knee became enduring symbol of Native suffering

front: What was the Carlisle boarding school system?
p1: Carlisle Indian Industrial School (Pennsylvania, 1879): Colonel Richard Pratt — 'kill the Indian, save the man' → children forbidden to speak languages, practice traditions or wear traditional clothing
p2: Scale: 100,000+ children forced in by early 1900s → death rates 30-50% from neglect, abuse and malnutrition → Navajo students: 13 cents/day for lunch vs recommended 50 cents
p3: Long-term trauma: graduates returned alienated from both worlds → boarding schools weakened matriarchal structures → cultural trauma passed through generations → contributed to high alcoholism and suicide rates on reservations

front: What was the role of Helen Hunt Jackson and the Indian Rights Association?
p1: 'A Century of Dishonour' (1881): Helen Hunt Jackson documented U.S. government's systematic treaty violations and mistreatment of Native Americans → presented to every member of Congress
p2: Indian Rights Association (IRA, 1882): white campaign group → advocated for Native rights and fair treatment → AIDA (1923): John Collier founded
p3: Paradox: IRA and reform groups meant well → BUT actively promoted assimilation policies (allotment, boarding schools) that destroyed what they claimed to protect

front: What was the significance of the Society of American Indians (SAI, 1911)?
p1: SAI (Society of American Indians, 1911): first pan-tribal organisation led by educated, assimilated Natives → lawyers, doctors, teachers → advocated for Native rights within American political system.
p2: Debated: full assimilation into American society vs tribal sovereignty → divisions between those who wanted citizenship rights and those who wanted to preserve separate tribal identity.
p3: Limited impact: small, elite membership — not representative of reservation populations → collapsed by 1920s → BUT educated Native leadership it produced became backbone of later NCAI (1944).

front: What was the impact of WWI service on Native Americans?
p1: WWI: 12,000 Native Americans served — many not yet citizens → demonstrated loyalty despite lack of rights → Citizenship Act (1924): all Native Americans granted citizenship.
p2: BUT: states blocked voting → Arizona and New Mexico refused to recognise Native voting rights → Harrison v Laveen (1948): Arizona finally forced to recognise.
p3: No improvement in land rights or living conditions → Meriam Report (1928): 82% below poverty line → WWI service produced no policy change.

front: What was the significance of the Indian Citizenship Act (1924)?
p1: Indian Citizenship Act (1924): citizenship granted to all Native Americans → BUT two-thirds already citizens through Dawes Act, military service or individual treaties.
p2: States blocked voting: Arizona and New Mexico refused to recognise Native voting rights → Harrison v Laveen (1948): Arizona finally forced to recognise.
p3: Citizenship without rights: no practical political power → reservations controlled by BIA → poverty unchanged → hollow without enforcement.

front: What was the significance of AIDA, the Leavitt Bill and Meriam Report?
p1: AIDA (1923): Collier founded → blocked Leavitt Bill (1926): 'Dance Order' seeking to ban Pueblo religious dances → first significant non-Native cultural protection victory.
p2: Meriam Report (1928): documented appalling poverty, disease, boarding school death rates, failure of Dawes Act → directly led to IRA (1934) → called for end to allotment.
p3: 82% of Native Americans below poverty line by 1928 → tuberculosis 25% above national average → boarding school death rates 30-50% → made federal inaction politically untenable.

front: What did the Indian Reorganization Act (Wheeler-Howard Act, 1934) do?
p1: Wheeler-Howard Act (1934): halted Dawes Act allotment → recovered unallocated land → restored 4 million of 90 million acres lost → established tribal constitutions and elected tribal councils
p2: Economic improvements: CCC-ID employed 85,000 Native Americans 1933-42 → planted 25 million trees, built 6,500 miles of road
p3: Significance: decisive ideological shift from assimilation to self-determination → reversed 50 years of federal policy → BUT 82% of Native Americans still below poverty line by 1940

front: What were the limitations of the Indian Reorganization Act (1934)?
p1: Collier's approach failed to account for Native diversity → policies based on Pueblo and Navajo experience → 25% of tribes rejected IRA outright → presumed all wanted same form of self-determination.
p2: Navajo rejected IRA: livestock reduction 1933-36 → 150,000 sheep, goats and horses killed → sheep were women's property in matrilineal Navajo society → economic and cultural devastation.
p3: Chronic underfunding: 82% below poverty line by 1940 → only $2 million annually for land buyback → boarding schools continued → paternalism did not end with Collier.

front: What was the role of the NCAI and Indian Claims Commission?
p1: NCAI (National Congress of American Indians, 1944): first large-scale pan-tribal advocacy organisation → founded to oppose Termination Policy and protect Native rights
p2: Indian Claims Commission (1946-78): created to resolve land claims → tribes could seek compensation — not land return → awarded $800 million total
p3: Limits: NCAI could not prevent Termination (1953) → Claims Commission offered money not sovereignty → showed legal route alone insufficient → AIM's direct action (1968+) addressed what NCAI could not

front: What was the significance of the Navajo Code Talkers and Ira Hayes?
p1: Navajo Code Talkers: 400-500 Navajo marines used Navajo language as unbreakable military code → critical to Pacific theatre → Japanese never broke it → classified until 1968.
p2: Ira Hayes (Pima): one of six men photographed raising flag at Iwo Jima → iconic image → returned home to Arizona to face poverty and discrimination → died destitute 1955 at 32.
p3: 44,000 Native Americans served → Indian Citizenship Act (1924) gave formal citizenship → BUT states still blocked voting → Harrison v Laveen (1948): Arizona finally recognised Native voting rights.

front: What was the Termination Policy (1953) and what were its consequences?
p1: Termination Policy (1953-68): ended federal recognition for 109 tribes → sold their lands, terminated healthcare, education and legal protections → Menominee (Wisconsin) and Klamath (Oregon) worst affected.
p2: Consequences: extreme poverty → terminated tribes lost all federal support → many lost land to private developers → Menominee hospital closed → malnutrition rates soared.
p3: NCAI lobbied against termination → Nixon formally ended it (1970) → Menominee Restoration Act (1973): first tribe restored → showed termination had been catastrophic failure.

front: What was the Indian Relocation Act (1956) and what were its consequences?
p1: Indian Relocation Act (1956): BIA provided one-way bus tickets to cities — Chicago, Los Angeles, Denver → promised jobs and housing → by 1970: 40% of Native Americans living in cities.
p2: Reality: urban poverty often replaced reservation poverty → housing substandard → jobs scarce → cultural isolation — no tribal community or BIA follow-up.
p3: AIM (1968) founded in Minneapolis by urban Natives who had experienced relocation → direct line from Relocation Act to AIM militancy.

front: What was the significance of the NIYC (1961) and the fish-ins?
p1: NIYC (National Indian Youth Council, 1961): first militant pan-tribal youth organisation → fish-ins (1964): asserted treaty fishing rights in Pacific Northwest — violated state law deliberately.
p2: Arrests → national media coverage → Marlon Brando joined protest → Puyallup and Nisqually tribes citing 1850s treaties guaranteeing fishing rights.
p3: Predated Black Power as militant model → eventually won in US v Washington (1974): tribes had right to 50% of fish catch.

front: What was the significance of AIM's founding (1968) and early actions?
p1: AIM (American Indian Movement) founded Minneapolis 1968: Dennis Banks and Clyde Bellecourt → urban Natives who had experienced police brutality and poverty
p2: Early actions: BIA headquarters occupied (1972) — Trail of Broken Treaties → 20-point manifesto demanding treaty enforcement and land restoration → Mount Rushmore occupation (1971)
p3: Significance: pan-tribal militant identity → united urban and reservation Natives → media-savvy confrontational tactics brought national attention

front: What was the significance of the Alcatraz Occupation (1969–71)?
p1: Led by Richard Oakes (Mohawk) and 'Indians of All Tribes' → occupied Alcatraz November 1969 → claimed 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty gave Natives right to unused federal land
p2: 19-month occupation → 10,000 Natives visited → generated massive national media coverage and public sympathy → demanded federal land for Native university, cultural centre and museum
p3: Limits: Richard Oakes' daughter died in fall during occupation (1970) → Oakes left → occupation ended 1971 without policy changes → BUT sparked Red Power movement nationally

front: What was the significance of the Wounded Knee Occupation (1973)?
p1: 71-day standoff at Wounded Knee, South Dakota (1973): AIM members and Oglala Lakota occupied the town
p2: Federal forces surrounded the town → negotiations held but government refused to discuss treaty rights → two Native activists killed → 600+ arrested → Wilson's GOON squad terrorised reservation throughout
p3: Significance: brought international attention to Native rights — compared by some to Selma → exposed BIA corruption → BUT 600+ arrested, leaders tried for years → movement fragmented afterwards

front: What was the significance of AIRFA and the Indian Child Welfare Act?
p1: AIRFA (1978): protected right to practice traditional religions → reversed decades of ceremony bans — Sun Dance, Ghost Dance suppressed since 1880s → allowed access to sacred sites.
p2: ICWA (1978): prevented removal of Native children to non-Native homes → tribal authority over child welfare → addressed systematic removal that had destroyed cultural transmission.
p3: BUT: AIRFA had no enforcement mechanism → 70% of Native religious leaders still reported struggles by 1992 → Graves Protection Act (1990): 10,000 sacred items and remains returned.

front: What was the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act and position by 1992?
p1: Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (1988): tribes could operate casinos without state interference → 150 casinos generating $1 billion+ annually by early 1990s → first major economic opportunity for some tribes.
p2: 200+ tribes administered own federal programmes under Self-Determination Act (1975) → NARF secured land and adoption rights → ICWA (1978) gave tribes child welfare jurisdiction.
p3: BUT: 25% of Native families still below poverty line in 1992 → 60% economically reliant on federal assistance → gaming wealth concentrated in some tribes, not universal.

front: What was the position of Native American rights in 1865?
p1: By 1865: Plains tribes — Sioux, Cheyenne, Comanche — still controlled vast territories → buffalo herds: 30 million → treaty system theoretically recognised tribal sovereignty.
p2: Manifest Destiny ideology: white settlement divinely ordained → Social Darwinism: Natives 'backward' → Indian Appropriations Act (1871) would end treaty-making — not yet passed.
p3: Economy: buffalo central — food, clothing, shelter, spiritual practice → before railroad and systematic slaughter → before Dawes Act → before boarding schools → about to collapse entirely.

front: What was the impact of Japanese internment on Native lands?
p1: WWII Japanese internment: Poston internment camp built on Colorado River Indian Reservation without tribal consent → 17,000 Japanese Americans housed on Navajo and Mohave lands.
p2: Harrison v Laveen (1948): Arizona recognised Native voting rights — last state to do so → 44,000 Native Americans had served in WWII, strengthening citizenship claims.
p3: BUT Termination Policy (1953) immediately reversed post-war progress → 109 tribes terminated → economic base destroyed.

front: What was the significance of US v Sioux Nation (1980) and NARF (1970)?
p1: US v Sioux Nation (1980): Black Hills illegally seized in 1877 → $106 million awarded → Sioux refused: 'The Black Hills are not for sale'
p2: Oneida v Oneida (1974): Oneida Nation could sue for land claims under federal treaties → precedent for dozens of tribal land claims
p3: Fisher v Montana (1976): tribes decide on adoptions → Bryan v Itasca (1976): states cannot tax reservations → Seminole v Butterworth (1982): tribal casino sovereignty

front: What was the position of Native American rights by 1992?
p1: By 1992: per capita income half national average → unemployment 50-80% on many reservations → 25% below poverty line → 60% economically reliant on federal assistance.
p2: Political: Self-Determination Act (1975): 200+ tribes administering own programmes → Gaming Act (1988): economic opportunity for some → sovereignty legally recognised but practically limited.
p3: Cultural: AIRFA (1978) protected religious practices → ICWA (1978): tribal child welfare jurisdiction → Graves Protection Act (1990): 10,000 items returned → languages partially revived.

front: Why did Southern elites introduce voter suppression in the Gilded Age?
p1: Populist Party threat: 1892 election — Populists won 5 states, 8.5% of vote. Dividing white vote
p2: Economic control: disenfranchising African Americans maintained dependence on white landowners as sharecroppers — political exclusion enforced economic exploitation. Racial hierarchy underpinned plantation economy.
p3: Legal cover: Mississippi v Williams (1898)

front: How was voter suppression implemented in the Gilded Age?
p1: Literacy tests: required voters to interpret complex constitutional clauses → administered selectively — passed illiterate whites, failed educated Black Americans → poll taxes: fees most Black sharecroppers could not afford.
p2: Grandfather clauses: exempted men whose grandfathers had voted before 1867 — excluded all former slaves → white-only Democratic primaries introduced 1890s
p3: Mississippi v Williams (1898): Supreme Court upheld these tactics → US v Guinn (1915) later struck down grandfather clauses → by 1900 Black voter turnout in South less than 5%.

front: What was the impact of bifurcation on African American society?
p1: Affirmative action + CRM → growing Black middle class: 40% of African Americans middle class by 1980s. White-collar jobs: 5% (1960)
p2: But gains deeply uneven: bifurcation created socioeconomic divide within Black community. Many concentrated in ghettoes — high unemployment, poor housing, underfunded schools. By 1992: Black families earned 60% of white income. Black unemployment 14.2% vs 6.6% white.
p3: War on Drugs (Nixon 1971, expanded Reagan 1980s): disproportionately targeted Black communities

front: What was laissez-faire and why was it harmful to workers?
