p1: Laissez-faire: dominant Gilded Age ideology — government must not interfere in business or labour relations. Courts, federal and state governments consistently sided with employers
p2: Consequences: Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) aimed at monopolies but used against unions. Court injunctions stopped strikes — Pullman (1894) ruled illegal. National Guard used 23 times in 1892 alone
p3: Persistence: survived into Progressive Era — Lochner (1905), Coppage (1915), Adkins (1923) all upheld 'freedom of contract'

front: What was collective bargaining and why did it matter?
p1: Collective bargaining: unions negotiate wages, hours and conditions on behalf of all workers — power individual workers lacked alone
p2: Gilded Age: AFL made gains through voluntary bargaining with Hanna and JP Morgan — exceptional cases, not the norm. Most employers refused outright
p3: Impact: union membership 3.7 million (1933) → 9 million (1938). By 1960s AFL-CIO members earned 20% more than non-unionised workers — direct product of collective bargaining.

front: How did employers suppress unions in the Gilded Age?
p1: Pinkertons: Carnegie Steel employed 300 armed Pinkerton agents at Homestead (1892) — arrived by barge, violent clash, 12 men dead. Companies hired private militias to break strikes
p2: Blacklisting: shared among 50 mine operators in Pennsylvania — known union organisers could not find work
p3: Company towns: Pullman controlled housing, rents and wages — could evict strikers. Welfare capitalism (1920s): employer-provided pensions and healthcare

front: What was the Sherman Antitrust Act and how was it used against unions?
p1: Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): passed to break up monopolies — Carnegie, Rockefeller. Aimed to prevent illegal restraints of trade. BUT rarely enforced against monopolies — government sided with big business.
p2: Used against unions: courts ruled strikes and boycotts were illegal restraints of trade. Pullman Strike (1894): injunction based on Sherman Act — halted strike, imprisoned Debs
p3: Clayton Antitrust Act (1914): attempted to exempt unions — labour not a commodity. BUT Duplex v Deering (1921) limited its impact

front: What was the story of the Homestead Strike (1892)?
p1: July 1892: Carnegie left for Scotland; Frick cut wages and locked out workers. Amalgamated Association organised defence of plant
p2: Workers fought back with rifles and cannons — 12 killed, Pinkertons surrendered. Governor Pattison then deployed 8,000 state militia — workers lost control of plant
p3: Strike collapsed November 1892. All rehired without union recognition. Carnegie praised Frick in private. Publicly maintained he supported workers — hypocrisy exposed by strike. Alexander Berkman imprisoned 22 years.

front: What was the story and significance of the Pullman Strike (1894)?
p1: Pullman Palace Car cut wages 25% — did not reduce rents in company housing. Debs' ARU boycotted Pullman cars
p2: 12,000 federal troops sent despite Governor Altgeld's objection. 30 deaths. Debs imprisoned for contempt. AFL refused to support ARU — exposed skilled/unskilled division.
p3: First use of federal injunction to break a strike — precedent used for decades. Federal government sided with corporations through courts and troops. Debs' imprisonment radicalised him

front: How did courts obstruct union rights? (Lochner, Coppage, Deering, Adkins)
p1: Freedom of contract doctrine: courts ruled employers and workers had equal right to set terms → ignored massive power imbalance
p2: Coppage v Kansas (1915): upheld yellow-dog contracts → Duplex v Deering (1921): upheld injunctions against secondary boycotts → Adkins v Children's Hospital (1923): struck down minimum wage for women.
p3: Not until NLRA v Jones & Laughlin (1937) confirmed Wagner Act constitutional did this shift → Norris-LaGuardia (1932) had already banned yellow-dog contracts — tide turned only with New Deal.

front: What made Cesar Chavez a significant leader?
p1: Chavez organised Filipino and Mexican American farm workers — historically excluded from NLRA, no union representation. UFW (1966): first successful farm workers' union
p2: Tactics: nonviolent strikes, consumer boycotts and fasting — modelled on Gandhi. Delano Grape Strike (1965–70): nationwide grape boycott built broad public support. Fasting drew Robert Kennedy's support
p3: Legacy: California Agricultural Labor Relations Act (1975) — first U.S. law protecting farm workers' collective bargaining rights. Direct product of UFW pressure. Expanded labour movement beyond white male industrial base

front: What was the story and significance of the Salad Bowl Strike?
p1: Filipino farm workers, California vegetable fields — supported by Mexican and other ethnic groups within UFW. Struck against low wages, poor conditions and exploitation of migrant workers in California's agricultural industry.
p2: Tactics: boycotts, marches, picketing, international solidarity — Chavez connected strike to civil rights and human dignity. Lettuce boycott spread nationally. International labour solidarity pressured growers.
p3: Success: better wages and union recognition. Alongside Delano Grape Strike, directly contributed to California Agricultural Labor Relations Act (1975). Showed nonviolent direct action could win rights for previously unorganised, vulnerable migrant workers.

front: What was the story of the Flint Sit-Down Strike (1936–37)?
p1: General Motors, Flint, Michigan — CIO organised sit-down strike December 1936 → workers occupied factory rather than picketing → impossible to bring in replacements without destroying machinery.
p2: 40,000 workers → Michigan Governor Murphy refused to deploy National Guard → GM sought court injunction — judge revealed he owned GM stock → 'Battle of Bulls Run' repulsed.
p3: After 44 days GM recognised UAW → inspired 200 more sit-down strikes in 1937 → NLRB v Fansteel (1939) later ruled sit-downs illegal.

front: What was the experience of workers during WWII?
p1: NWLB (1942): government worked with AFL and CIO — mediated disputes, upheld codes of practice, prevented strike action. Union membership peaked 35% of workforce (14.8 million) by 1945
p2: Smith-Connally Act (1943): government could seize industries threatened by strikes — passed over FDR's veto. AFL and CIO agreed no-strike pledges in exchange for recognition and wartime wages
p3: Limits: NWLB policies only benefited AFL and CIO — excluded unaffiliated workers. Benefits uneven for African Americans despite EO 8802. No-strike pledges suppressed grievances

front: What was the post-WWII strike wave and how did it lead to Taft-Hartley?
p1: 1946: 5,000 strikes, 4.6 million workers — largest strike wave in U.S. history. Pent-up pressure from wartime no-strike pledges. Steel, auto, coal, railways all struck simultaneously
p2: Taft-Hartley Act (1947): passed over Truman's veto — direct response to strike wave. Banned secondary strikes and closed shops. Allowed right-to-work laws — 21 states enacted, primarily South and West
p3: Impact: anti-communist oaths weakened CIO — leaders who refused lost NLRB access. McCarthyism compounded effect. Taft-Hartley began rollback from 35% membership peak

front: What was workers' experience during the 1950s–60s boom?
p1: AFL-CIO merged 1955 — 16 million members, 85% of unionised workforce. Members earned 20% more than non-unionised workers by 1960s
p2: Kennedy EO 10988 (1962): federal employees right to unionise. Civil Rights Act (1964): prohibited employment discrimination by race, sex or national origin
p3: Automation threat: manufacturing jobs declining — blue-collar unions weakened. New electronics and service sectors relocated to avoid unions. By 1979 manufacturing down 40% from 1970 peak

front: What was Manifest Destiny and its impact on Native Americans?
p1: Manifest Destiny: 19th century ideology — white American settlement of continent from coast to coast divinely ordained → provided moral and religious justification for Native displacement.
p2: Social Darwinism: framed Native Americans as 'backward' on inferior civilisation rung → eugenic theories seen as modern science → justified racial separation and cultural destruction as progress.
p3: Underpinned Plains Wars, Dawes Act, boarding schools → settlers not stealing land — fulfilling divine purpose → IRA (1882): white missionaries saw assimilation as Christian duty.

front: What was the reservation system and how did it work?
p1: Reservation system: federal policy confining Native tribes to designated land areas → managed by BIA → began with Indian Removal Act (1830s), systematised after Plains Wars.
p2: BIA took increasing control — corrupt and paternalistic → reservations frequently on poor, infertile land → Natives dependent on insufficient government rations → tuberculosis 25% above national average.
p3: By 1900 only 100,000 of 240,000 Plains Indians remained → Dawes Act (1887) broke up even reservation land → 'ghettos in the wilderness' — economic dependency replacing self-sufficiency.

front: What was the significance of the buffalo extermination?
p1: Buffalo: central to Plains tribes — food, clothing, shelter, tools, spiritual practice. Federal government encouraged systematic slaughter to force Natives onto reservations. U.S. Army killed estimated 10 million buffalo 1865–1883.
p2: Scale: buffalo population 30 million (1860)
p3: Impact: Plains tribes lost economic independence

front: What was the Long Walk of the Navajo (1864–66)?
p1: Kit Carson destroyed Navajo crops, orchards and livestock — forced surrender. 8,000–9,000 Navajo forced on 300-mile march to Bosque Redondo reservation, New Mexico — winter conditions. Thousands died from starvation, exposure and disease en route.
p2: Bosque Redondo: barren, alkaline soil, contaminated water — crops failed repeatedly. 3,000 Navajo died in four years from disease and starvation. Government rationing inadequate, BIA agents corrupt.
p3: Treaty of 1868: Navajo allowed to return to ancestral lands — one of the few treaty victories of the period. Reservation expanded 4 million

front: What was the significance of Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull?
p1: Sitting Bull (Hunkpapa Lakota): spiritual leader → refused to sign treaties → led Black Hills resistance → vision at Little Bighorn inspired warriors → killed by Indian police 1890.
p2: Crazy Horse (Oglala Lakota): military leader → refused reservation life → led warriors at Little Bighorn — annihilated Custer's 7th Cavalry → surrendered 1877 → killed at Fort Robinson.
p3: Little Bighorn (1876): only major Native military victory → BUT both killed after surrender → Black Hills lost → Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) followed.

front: What was the significance of the Black Hills to the Sioux?
p1: Black Hills (Paha Sapa): sacred to Sioux → Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868): guaranteed Black Hills 'in perpetuity' → gold discovered 1874 → Sioux refused to sell.
p2: 1877: Black Hills seized in violation of treaty → government threatened to stop rations → Mount Rushmore (1927-41) carved into sacred land without consent.
p3: US v Sioux Nation (1980): $106 million awarded → Sioux refused → fund grown to $600m+ by 1992, still unclaimed.

front: What was the Indian Appropriations Act (1871)?
p1: Indian Appropriations Act (1871): tribes no longer recognised as independent nations → ended treaty-making → tribes became 'wards of the state'
p2: Practical consequences: BIA took increasing control → corrupt and paternalistic → tribes lost legal standing — could not sue in federal courts
p3: Lone Wolf v Hitchcock (1903): Congress could unilaterally revoke even existing treaties → combined with 1871 Act: removed both future treaty protection AND past treaty protection

front: What was the impact of reservations on Native Americans? (positives)
p1: Reservations allowed tribal life to continue in limited forms — cultural identity and community sustained. Better healthcare than nomadic lifestyle, albeit very limited. Some Native Americans gained jobs as interpreters, scouts or Indian Agency workers.
p2: Navajo success: reservation expanded 4 million → 10.5 million acres. Sheep and goats: 15,000 → 1.7 million. Population: 8,000 (1868)
p3: Reservations provided territorial base for later political campaigns — NCAI (1944), AIM (1968) all built from reservation communities. Even limited sovereignty became foundation for self-determination claims.

front: What was the impact of reservations on Native Americans? (limitations)
p1: Land infertile, difficult to farm → many dependent on insufficient government rations → late 1880s: government cut meat subsidies to Sioux — starvation → by 1900 only 100,000 of 240,000 Plains Indians remained.
p2: BIA corrupt: agents stole rations, manipulated accounts → 1871 Act abolished tribal sovereignty → no legal recourse → reservations became 'ghettos in the wilderness'.
p3: Cultural destruction: hunting and leadership roles removed → matriarchal tribes: women lost status as Dawes Act gave land to male heads of families → Sun Dance, Ghost Dance suppressed.

front: What were the positive effects of assimilation policies on Native Americans?
p1: Boarding schools: vocational training — domestic skills for girls, trade skills for boys → some graduates employed as Indian Agency office workers, interpreters or army scouts.
p2: Dawes Act (1887): 160 acres per family head → landowners became taxpayers, gained citizenship rights → Five Civilised Tribes exempt from Dawes Act until Curtis Act (1898) — retained significant self-determination.
p3: Some assimilated Natives gained access to wider society → lawyers, doctors, teachers who later advocated for Native rights → SAI (1911) founded by educated, assimilated Natives.

front: What were the damaging effects of assimilation policies on Native Americans?
p1: Cultural destruction: Sun Dance banned, buffalo hunting forbidden → boarding schools: 100,000+ children by early 1900s → forbidden to speak languages or practice traditions
p2: Language loss: 75% of Native American languages lost by 1930 → land loss: 156 million acres (1881) → 78 million acres by 1890
p3: Long-term trauma: graduates returned alienated from both worlds → matriarchal structures weakened → high alcoholism and suicide rates on reservations

front: What was the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) and why was it significant?
p1: Ghost Dance (1889): Wovoka — 5 days of dance to reconnect with ancestors and restore lost lands → spread rapidly across Plains → Army alarmed by mass gatherings
p2: December 29, 1890: 7th Cavalry surrounded Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek → shot fired, possibly accidentally → cavalry opened fire → 250+ Lakota killed — men, women and children
p3: Significance: end of armed Plains Indian resistance → Ghost Dance suppressed — last major cultural resistance movement → AIM chose Wounded Knee deliberately for 1973 occupation.

front: What was the role of the Five Civilised Tribes and Sequoyah Convention?
p1: Five Civilised Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole): written constitutions, elected governments, mixed economy → occupied Indian Territory (Oklahoma) → exempt from Dawes Act allotment until Curtis Act (1898).
p2: Curtis Act (1898): ended Five Civilised Tribes' governments → allotment imposed → Muskogee/Sequoyah Convention (1905): leaders proposed all-Native state of Sequoyah — own governor and Congressional representatives
p3: Congress rejected Sequoyah → Oklahoma created 1907, merging Indian Territory with Oklahoma Territory → showed Native Americans could govern successfully on own terms

front: What was the role of BIA corruption and paternalism?
p1: BIA (Bureau of Indian Affairs): tribes became 'wards of state' after Indian Appropriations Act (1871) → no legal standing
p2: Structural consequences: BIA controlled access to schools, healthcare, employment, housing → late 1880s: government cut meat subsidies to Sioux → starvation → Dawes Act allotment poorly administered
p3: Trail of Broken Treaties (1972): AIM occupied BIA headquarters — symbolised BIA as enemy → Nixon ended termination (1970) → began shifting power from BIA to tribes

front: What was the significance of John Collier and the AIDA?
p1: John Collier: lived among Pueblo communities in New Mexico 1920s → founded AIDA (1923) → blocked Leavitt Bill (1926): 'Dance Order' seeking to ban Pueblo religious dances.
p2: Commissioner for Indian Affairs (1933-45): drove Indian Reorganization Act (1934) → ended allotment, encouraged tribal self-governance, protected cultural practices.
p3: Limits: policies based on Pueblo and Navajo experience → didn't suit all tribes → Navajo rejected IRA due to livestock reduction → 25% of tribes rejected IRA outright.

front: What was the role of the IECW/CCC-ID in the New Deal?
p1: IECW/CCC-ID: New Deal employment for Native Americans → 85,000 employed 1933-42 → planted 25 million trees, built 6,500 miles of road → surplus army clothing distributed
p2: Cultural: Indian Arts and Crafts Board (1935): revived Native arts as economic ventures → cultural education funding up 65% (1935-40) → tribal councils reinstated → ceremonial dance bans overturned
p3: Limits: Navajo students 13 cents/day for lunch vs recommended 50 cents → only $2 million annually to buy back lost land

front: What was the Navajo livestock reduction and why did it matter?
p1: Navajo sheep and goat herds: 1.7 million — central to economy, culture and identity → Collier and federal scientists believed overgrazing destroying Navajo land → government ordered livestock reduction 1933-36
p2: Navajo experience: sheep were wealth, spiritual connection and family heritage → their destruction was economic and cultural devastation → women especially affected — Navajo society matrilineal, sheep traditionally women's property
p3: Consequence: Navajo rejected IRA (1934) outright → tribe Collier most wanted to help refused because of livestock reduction

front: What was the impact of reservation poverty as a structural condition?
p1: 1960s-70s: per capita income half national average → unemployment on many reservations exceeded 50%, sometimes 80% → few roads, schools, hospitals or utilities → many homes lacked running water.
p2: LBJ 'Forgotten Americans' speech (1968): 'the most deprived and forgotten group' → War on Poverty programmes launched → Indian Relocation Act (1956) pushed many to cities — urban poverty often replaced reservation poverty.
p3: Gaming Act (1988): began creating economic opportunities → but 25% of Native American families still below poverty line in 1992 → 60% economically reliant on federal assistance.

front: What was Red Power and how did it differ from earlier activism?
p1: Red Power: militant movement for Native rights → emerged late 1960s, inspired by Black Power → emphasised Native pride, sovereignty and cultural revival → rejected gradualist legal approach of NCAI
p2: AIM (1968): red berets and leather jackets modelled on Black Panthers → fish-ins (1968), Alcatraz (1969-71), Trail of Broken Treaties (1972), Wounded Knee (1973)
p3: Impact: Nixon ended Termination (1970) → Indian Self-Determination Act (1975) — both partly responses to Red Power pressure → BUT AIM militancy vs NCAI legal approach created tensions

front: How did Black Power influence Red Power?
p1: Direct influence: AIM (1968) modelled on Black Panthers — red berets, leather jackets → 'Red Power' directly inspired by 'Black Power'
p2: Limits: Native activism pre-dated Black Power → NIYC (1961) fish-ins already underway → NCAI (1944) established → Great Society and War on Poverty laid groundwork independently
p3: Alcatraz (1969): 10,000 Natives visited — media impact mirrored Panthers' → BUT sovereignty claims were specifically about land and treaty rights — not civil rights integration

front: What was the significance of the Trail of Broken Treaties (1972)?
p1: November 1972: cross-country caravan of multiple tribes drove to Washington DC before presidential election → demanded restoration of Native sovereignty and treaty-making rights → occupied BIA headquarters for several days.
p2: 20-point manifesto: treaty enforcement, restoration of tribal land base, abolition of BIA, new treaty relationships → Nixon administration negotiated rather than use force — election timing made confrontation politically costly
p3: Significance: most effective pan-tribal organisation in Red Power era → BIA occupation symbolically powerful → led directly to Wounded Knee (1973)

front: What was the significance of Nixon ending termination and the Self-Determination Act?
p1: Nixon (1970): formally ended termination — acknowledged it had been wrong. Federal government had trust responsibility to Native Americans
p2: Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (1975): tribes could administer own education, health and welfare programmes using federal funds. Shift away from BIA control
p3: Limits: federal government still controlled funding — 60% of Native Americans economically reliant on federal assistance by 1992. Sovereignty legally recognised but practically limited by ongoing federal oversight

front: What was the significance of NARF and Oneida v Oneida (1974)?
p1: NARF (Native American Rights Fund, 1970): provided legal representation for tribes → fighting for treaty enforcement, land claims and sovereignty in federal courts.
p2: Oneida v Oneida (1974): Oneida Nation could sue for land claims under federal treaties → precedent for dozens of tribal land claims → NARF used this to pursue land rights.
p3: Fisher v Montana (1976): tribal courts decide on adoptions → Bryan v Itasca (1976): states cannot tax reservations → built tribal sovereignty case by case.

front: What was the significance of the Indian Child Welfare Act (1978)?
p1: Context: since boarding school era, Native children systematically removed → placed in white foster and adoptive homes → by 1970s: 25-35% of all Native children separated from families.
p2: ICWA (1978): prevented removal of Native children to non-Native homes → tribal authority over child welfare cases → required active efforts to keep children within extended family and community.
p3: Fisher v Montana (1976) had established tribal court adoption jurisdiction → ICWA built on this → addressed ongoing cultural destruction that boarding schools had represented in a new form.

front: What was coverture?
p1: Legal doctrine: married woman's identity subsumed into husband's → could not own property, sign contracts or keep wages → no legal recourse against abusive husbands → divorce deeply stigmatised.
p2: Effects: husbands controlled all marital property and earnings → women could not run businesses, take loans or appear in court independently → married women had no independent legal existence.
p3: Erosion: Married Women's Property Acts — state reforms from 1870s. Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974): women's right to independent credit. ERA failed (1982) → no constitutional end to all coverture-based discrimination.

front: What was the cult of domesticity?
p1: Separate spheres: men in public sphere — politics, business, law → women confined to private sphere — home, children, moral guardianship → women expected to be pious, pure, domestic, submissive.
p2: Consequences: women's campaigns had to be framed as 'moral' concerns to be acceptable → temperance, abolitionism, settlement houses → 1 in 5 women died in childbirth
p3: Persistence: Dr Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946) — 23 million copies → reinforced 1950s housewife ideal → Friedan's Feminine Mystique (1963) named the ideology's psychological damage

front: What were the Comstock Laws (1873)?
p1: Comstock Laws (1873): federal legislation making distribution of 'obscene' materials through mail illegal → explicitly included contraceptive information and abortion materials → enforced aggressively for nearly a century.
p2: Impact: Sanger's Brooklyn clinic (1916) shut down after serving 20,000 women → distribution of contraceptive information to anyone, even doctors, was federal crime
p3: Legacy: Comstock Laws were primary federal obstacle to reproductive rights for 90 years → access remained deeply unequal — urban wealthy women found informal means, poor rural women could not

front: What were the key ideas of the Feminine Mystique (1963)?
p1: Friedan identified 'the problem with no name' → college-educated suburban housewives' profound unhappiness in prescribed domestic role → described marriage as a 'comfortable concentration camp'
p2: Argument: post-war society trapped women in domesticity → constructed by advertisers, Freudian psychologists and women's magazines → kept women out of public life and consuming domestic products
p3: Impact: 3 million copies in 3 years → Friedan co-founded NOW (1966) → launched second-wave feminism

front: What was the significance of Susan B. Anthony?
p1: NWSA (1869): founded with Stanton → demanded federal constitutional amendment for women's suffrage → opposed 15th Amendment that excluded women → 20,000 members by 1890
p2: Anthony attempted to vote in Rochester (1872) → arrested → fined $100 → refused to pay → 'I shall never pay a dollar of your unjust penalty'
p3: Legacy: federal amendment strategy eventually succeeded — 19th Amendment (1920) → Anthony died 1906, 14 years before victory → BUT NWSA focused on white middle-class women

front: What was the significance of Frances Willard and the WCTU?
p1: WCTU (1874): Willard as leader from 1879 → 300,000 members by 1910 → largest women's organisation of era → Women's Crusade (1873): 50,000 women marched
p2: Campaign: successfully lobbied for 18th Amendment (1919) — Prohibition → showed women could win major political victories before gaining the vote → established women's moral authority in public sphere
p3: Limits: Prohibition was middle-class moral imposition on working-class and immigrant cultures → Molly Pitcher Club (1922) opposed it → 21st Amendment (1933) repealed Prohibition

front: What was the significance of Jane Addams and Hull House?
p1: Hull House (1889): founded in Chicago → 2,000+ people served per week by second year → largest settlement house in USA by 1900 → 400+ settlement houses nationwide by 1910
p2: Work: childcare, healthcare, job training, education, English classes for immigrant women → trained generation of women social reformers → National Consumers League (1899): Florence Kelley — Hull House-trained
p3: Limits: channelled women's energy into 'moral reform' within separate spheres ideology → Hull House focused on white immigrant women → Black women largely excluded

front: What was the significance of Carrie Chapman Catt and NAWSA?
p1: NAWSA (1890): merger of NWSA and AWSA under Catt → 'Winning Plan' (1916): combined state campaigns with federal amendment push → 2 million members by 1919
p2: 19th Amendment (1920): NAWSA's 50-year campaign succeeded → Catt founded League of Women Voters (1920) immediately after — to educate newly-enfranchised female electorate
p3: Limits: NAWSA prioritised white Southern women's support → Black women forced to march at back of 1913 Suffrage Parade

front: What was the significance of Alice Paul?
p1: CUWS (1913): Paul and Lucy Burns → militant tactics — picketed White House, hunger strikes, force-fed in prison → 1913 Suffrage Parade: 8,000 marched → kept pressure on Wilson throughout WWI.
p2: ERA (1923): introduced constitutional equality → reintroduced every Congress for 50 years → lobbied for sex to be included in Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII.
p3: ERA passed Congress (1972) — Paul aged 87 → failed ratification (1982) → three defining contributions: CUWS militant tactics, ERA, Title VII sex inclusion.

front: What was the significance of Margaret Sanger?
p1: Brooklyn clinic (1916): served 20,000 women → shut down for violating Comstock Laws → American Birth Control League (1921) → 222 clinics by 1941 → later renamed Planned Parenthood
p2: Tactics: deliberately violated Comstock Laws to force court cases → international speaking tours → argued birth control essential for women's health, economic independence and liberation
p3: Limits: access remained class-divided — urban wealthier women benefited most → some of Sanger's writings associated with eugenics → BUT 222 clinics overwhelmingly served working-class and immigrant women

front: What was the significance of Frances Perkins and Eleanor Roosevelt?
p1: Frances Perkins: first female Cabinet member — Secretary of Labour 1933-45 → shaped FLSA (1938): minimum wage, 44-hour week, child labour ban → shaped Social Security Act (1935).
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt: transformed First Lady role → press conferences, newspaper column → pushed FDR on appointments → resigned from DAR to support Marian Anderson (1939).
p3: BUT: 80% in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working → CCC excluded women → Social Security excluded domestic and agricultural workers — majority of women of colour.

front: What was the significance of Betty Friedan and NOW?
p1: NOW (1966): founded by Friedan → Miss America protest (1968): crowned a pig, symbolically rejected objectification → Women's Strike for Equality (1970): 50,000 marched in New York
p2: Lobbied for: Equal Pay Act (1963), Title VII enforcement, Title IX (1972), ERA ratification and reproductive rights
p3: Limits: NOW criticised as predominantly white and middle-class → focused on professional women's concerns → ignored working-class and Black women's specific struggles

front: What was the significance of Phyllis Schlafly and Stop ERA?
p1: Stop ERA (1972): Schlafly launched immediately after ERA passed Congress → argued ERA would eliminate protective legislation, force women into combat, require unisex bathrooms, destroy traditional family
p2: Tactics: mobilised conservative and working-class women → evangelical Christian women's organisations provided grassroots base → by 1982 only 35 of 38 states ratified → ERA dead
p3: Significance: showed conservative women's political mobilisation could match progressive women's → Schlafly herself a lawyer — used freedoms feminism had created to campaign against further feminist gains

front: What was the position of women in 1865?
p1: No vote at any level → coverture: husband controlled all property, contracts and wages → 5-7 children → 1 in 5 died in childbirth → only 3% attended college vs 25% of men.
p2: 15% employed outside home → 17% at half male wages → immigrant women: 70 hours/week in sweatshops → 40% of Black women in domestic service → 400,000+ Civil War widows with no safety net.
p3: KOL only union welcoming women → Comstock Laws (1873): criminalised contraceptive information → suffrage campaigns confined to 'moral' sphere.

front: What was the impact of Reconstruction on women's rights?
p1: 15th Amendment (1870): vote granted to Black men — excluded women → NWSA (Anthony/Stanton) opposed it → AWSA (Stone) supported it → split weakened suffrage movement for 20 years
p2: Anthony arrested voting in Rochester (1872) → $100 fine refused → Wyoming Territory granted female suffrage (1869) → Women's Crusade (1873): 50,000 marched → WCTU founded (1874)
p3: Black women excluded from both NWSA and AWSA → Reconstruction Congress focused entirely on African American male rights → women's suffrage treated as separate, secondary question

front: What were the educational and employment gains for women in the Gilded Age?
p1: Education: 111,000 in higher education by 1870 (21%) → 32% by 1880 → by 1900 half of all high school graduates were female
p2: Domestic technology: plumbing, heating, commercial laundries reduced household burdens → birth rate: 5.42 per family (1850) → 3.56 (1900) → some women entering professional roles.
p3: BUT: immigrant women: 70 hours/week for $5 → only 2% of trade unionists → education for middle-class women framed as preparation for marriage

front: What were working conditions like for women in the Gilded Age?
p1: Wages: half male wages throughout → immigrant women: 70 hours/week for $5 → 40% of Black women in domestic service — no union, no legal protection.
p2: AFL excluded women → 2% of trade unionists women by 1900 → 1882 Lawrence: textile women received no male union support → no minimum wage, no safety standards.
p3: WTUL (1903): first effort to organise women workers → Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911): 146 killed — owners locked exit doors → Bread and Roses (1912): 20,000 immigrant women, 15% pay rise.

front: What was the significance of the Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911)?
p1: New York City, March 1911 → fire on upper floors of Triangle Shirtwaist Factory → owners had locked exit doors
p2: 100,000 marched at victims' funeral → New York Factory Commission: comprehensive investigation led by Frances Perkins
p3: Significance: galvanised labour movement around women workers' safety → Perkins later used findings to shape New Deal legislation → showed male union neglect had lethal consequences

front: What was the significance of the Bread and Roses Strike (1912)?
p1: Lawrence, Massachusetts → mill owners cut wages after 54-hour work week law reduced hours → 20,000+ immigrant women struck — IWW-led → 51 nationalities
p2: Tactics: picketing, marches, children sent to union families in other cities — generated public sympathy → no male union support → Elizabeth Gurley Flynn central to leadership.
p3: Success: 15% pay rise, overtime pay, no discrimination against strikers → showed immigrant working-class women could win major industrial dispute through solidarity

front: What was the impact of WWI on women's rights?
p1: Employment: 40% of women employed during war → entered manufacturing, engineering, professional and technical roles previously closed to them
p2: Suffrage argument: women's wartime contribution made exclusion from democratic rights untenable → Lanham Act (1941) parallel: government later funded childcare for working mothers
p3: BUT: post-WWI retrenchment — majority returned to domestic roles → Red Scare framed female independence as threatening

front: What was the impact of the 19th Amendment (1920)?
p1: 19th Amendment (1920): vote granted after 50 years → BUT only 1/3 of women voted in 1920s vs 2/3 of men → Black women faced voter suppression in South.
p2: VRA (1965) made vote real for Black women → Mississippi Black women's registration: 6% (1964) → 60% (1969) → ERA (1923): introduced by Alice Paul — rejected.
p3: Women's Bureau (1920) — limited enforcement powers → Nellie Taylor Ross: first female governor (1925) → political impact of suffrage far less than suffragists hoped.

front: What was flapper culture and what did it represent?
p1: Flapper culture: young, urban, white, middle-class women — dancing, smoking, drinking, short hair, short skirts → challenge to Victorian femininity → birth rate falling, marriage age rising
p2: BUT: limited to white urban middle class → rural, working-class, Black and immigrant women unaffected or hostile
p3: 80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll: married women should not take men's jobs → Comstock Laws still in force

front: What were the gains for women during the New Deal?
p1: Perkins: first female Cabinet member → FLSA (1938): minimum wage, 44-hour week, child labour ban → WPA employed 400,000 women by 1938 → women union members 800,000 by 1940.
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt pushed FDR on appointments → Florence Allen: first female Circuit Court judge → Bethune: led NYA Negro Affairs → Aid to Dependent Children (1935): first federal support for single mothers.
p3: CIO more inclusive → 1937 Steelworkers' Strike: women played central organising roles → New Deal legal framework (NLRB, FLSA) later supported equal pay campaigns.

front: What were the limitations of the New Deal for women?
p1: FLSA (1938): female teachers earned 20% less than male in 1939 → CCC excluded women entirely → WPA: one-family-member policy favoured men → Social Security excluded domestic and agricultural workers.
p2: 80% in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working → Aid to Dependent Children reinforced motherhood role → New Deal assumed male breadwinner throughout.
p3: Black women excluded by white-administered Southern relief → Mexican American women vulnerable to deportation → rural women had least access to all programmes.

front: What was the impact of WWII on women's employment?
p1: 6 million women entered workforce during WWII → by 1944: 1 in 4 married women working → Rosie the Riveter → Lanham Act (1941): federal childcare funding for working mothers.
p2: 75% wanted to remain employed after WWII — distinct from post-WWI → entered industrial, professional and technical roles previously closed.
p3: BUT: 2 million lost jobs in 1946 as men returned → GI Bill: primarily benefited male veterans → women's undergraduate share: 40% (1920) → 30% (1950).

front: What was the significance of Dr Spock and the post-war housewife ideal?
p1: Dr Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946): 23 million copies → argued women should embrace nurturing role exclusively → reinforced 1950s suburban housewife as dominant cultural ideal.
p2: Cold War conformity: domestic sphere as women's patriotic duty → GI Bill reinforced male breadwinner → women's undergraduate share: 40% (1920) → 30% (1950).
p3: Pill approved FDA (1960) → 6 million using it by 1965 → began undermining domestic ideal → Feminine Mystique (1963) named what Dr Spock had helped create.

front: What was the Kennedy Commission on the Status of Women (1961)?
p1: Kennedy Commission (1961): Eleanor Roosevelt chaired → first federal body to document systematic sex discrimination
p2: Led directly to: Equal Pay Act (1963) — first federal legislation prohibiting pay discrimination by sex → women earning 59 cents per dollar in 1963
p3: Significance: first time federal government formally acknowledged and documented gender discrimination → broke from assumption that women's inequality was natural or acceptable → set legislative agenda for next decade

front: What was the significance of the Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII?
p1: Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: prohibited employment discrimination by sex → Alice Paul had lobbied for sex to be included → late addition but became one of most powerful legal tools.
p2: EEOC established to enforce → initial resistance: chairman called sex provision a 'fluke' → NOW (1966) formed partly to pressure EEOC to take sex discrimination seriously.
p3: Impact: opened professional roles to women → women could sue employers → combined with Equal Pay Act (1963): foundation for economic equality claims.

front: What was the significance of second-wave and radical feminism?
p1: Second-wave feminism: beyond suffrage → demanded economic, social and cultural equality → NOW (1966), Women's Strike for Equality (1970), Ms Magazine (1972)
p2: Radical feminism: Miss America protest (1968) — crowned a pig → Burial of True Womanhood at Arlington National Cemetery (1968) → 'The Feminists': called for abolition of marriage
p3: Tensions: radical feminism energised movement but also alienated moderates → sparked conservative backlash → Schlafly's Stop ERA mobilised around fear of radical feminism's implications

front: What was the significance of the Pill (1960)?
p1: Pill approved FDA (1960): 6 million women using it by 1965 → birth rate: 3.65 (1960) → 1.86 (1976) → marriage age: 20.3 (1960) → 23.3 (1980).
p2: Sexual revolution: women engaged sexually without fear of unwanted pregnancy → pursued education and careers without immediate family formation.
p3: BUT: initially only legal for married women → Griswold (1965) protected married couples → Eisenstadt (1972) extended to unmarried → working-class women had least access in early years.

front: What were Griswold v Connecticut (1965) and Eisenstadt v Baird (1972)?
p1: Griswold v Connecticut (1965): Supreme Court struck down state ban on contraceptives for married couples → right to marital privacy
p2: Eisenstadt v Baird (1972): extended contraceptive rights to unmarried individuals → built on Griswold → completed right to contraception regardless of marital status
p3: Significance: both decisions built on legal foundation Sanger had fought for since 1916 → overturned 90 years of Comstock Laws' reproductive suppression

front: What was the significance of Title IX (1972)?
p1: Title IX (1972): prohibited gender discrimination in federally funded education programmes → direct result of NOW lobbying → transformed women's access to higher education, professional training and sports.
p2: Impact: women's participation in college sports exploded → by 1992: women earning 40% of law degrees and 40% of medical degrees
p3: BUT: implementation slow and contested → male sports establishment resisted → Reagan era weakened enforcement → Title IX required ongoing litigation to enforce

front: What was the significance of Roe v Wade (1973)?
p1: Roe v Wade (1973): Supreme Court ruled right to abortion protected under constitutional right to privacy established in Griswold (1965) → invalidated most state abortion laws
p2: Context: National Organisation for Repeal of Abortion Laws (1969) had built pressure → combined with Griswold (1965) and Eisenstadt (1972): complete reproductive rights framework established in less than a decade.
p3: BUT: immediately polarising → National Right to Life Committee formed same year → Hyde Amendment (1976): federal abortion funding restricted — low-income women most affected

front: What was the political polarisation over abortion after Roe v Wade?
p1: Before Roe: abortion not a major partisan issue → both parties contained pro-choice and anti-abortion politicians.
p2: After Roe: National Right to Life Committee (1973) → Republican Party adopted anti-abortion platform → Reagan (1981-89): opposed abortion rights, made conservative Supreme Court appointments.
p3: By 1992: abortion primary gender issue splitting parties → Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992): Supreme Court allowed state restrictions — showed ongoing vulnerability of Roe.

front: What was the ERA and why did it fail?
p1: ERA: first proposed by Alice Paul (1923) → reintroduced every Congress for 50 years → passed Congress (1972): constitutional guarantee equal rights could not be denied on account of sex
p2: Schlafly's Stop ERA: argued ERA would eliminate protective legislation, force women into combat, destroy traditional family → mobilised conservative and religious women
p3: Significance: by 1992 no constitutional guarantee of sex equality in the USA → every legislative gain — Equal Pay Act, Title VII, Title IX — remained vulnerable

front: What was the anti-feminist backlash of the 1970s–80s?
p1: Schlafly stopped ERA (1982) → Moral Majority (1979): Falwell's evangelical political organisation → Reagan (1981-89): opposed ERA, abortion, Title IX enforcement
p2: Reagan welfare cuts disproportionately affected women — single mothers most vulnerable → PATCO (1981): fired 11,000 striking workers — weakened unions affecting women in unionised sectors
p3: BUT: backlash did not reverse all gains → 60% of women employed by 1992 → women outpacing men in graduation → 'Year of the Woman' (1992): 24 women to House

front: What was the position of women by 1992?
p1: Political: 55% women voted vs 49% men → 24 women to House (11%), 6 to Senate (5%) → O'Connor: first female Supreme Court Justice (1981) → ERA unratified.
p2: Social: 60% of women employed → average 2.2 children — lowest since 19th century → outpacing men in graduation: 84% vs 78% → 40% of law and medical degrees.
p3: Economic: women 40% of workforce → 75 cents per dollar → glass ceiling: only 10% of management → Roe under threat — Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992) allowed state restrictions.

front: What was the significance of WTUL and women in the labour movement?
p1: WTUL (1903): first sustained effort to organise women workers → Bread and Roses Strike (1912): IWW-led, WTUL supported → 15% pay rise → showed immigrant women could win major disputes.
p2: CLUW (1974): women's voice within AFL-CIO → pushed for equal pay → women's union membership: 800,000 by 1940 — 300% increase since 1930 → public sector unions increasingly women-led.
p3: BUT: AFL excluded women throughout → only 2% of trade unionists women by 1900 → deindustrialisation eliminated unionised manufacturing jobs → women in lower-paid service sector by 1992.

front: What were the gains for women during the Gilded Age?
p1: Education: 111,000 in higher education (21%) by 1870 → 32% by 1880 → half of all high school graduates female by 1900 → clerical employment grew tenfold → birth rate: 5.42 (1850) → 3.56 (1900).
p2: WCTU: 300,000 members by 1910 → Hull House (1889): 2,000+/week → state suffrage: Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, Idaho → National Consumer League (1899).
p3: BUT: no federal suffrage → immigrant women 70 hours/week for $5 → only 2% of trade unionists → Black women excluded from most gains.

front: What were the limits on women's progress during the Gilded Age?
p1: No federal suffrage → Minor v Happersett (1875) blocked route → only 4 states by 1900 → women paid half male wages → immigrant women: 70 hours/week for $5.
p2: Education gains for white middle class only → Black women excluded from mainstream suffrage → Comstock Laws blocked reproductive rights.
p3: 1882 Lawrence: no male union support → AFL excluded women → only 2% of trade unionists → temperance imposed middle-class values on working-class immigrant communities.

front: How effective were women's movements in the Gilded Age?
p1: NWSA: Anthony attempted to vote (1872) → arrested → $100 fine refused → national attention → AWSA: state victories — Wyoming, Colorado, Utah → NAWSA (1890) unified movement
p2: National Consumer League (1899): workplace safety advocacy → YWCA (1867): helped urban women → National Association of Coloured Women (1896): Ida B. Wells fought for Black women outside mainstream.
p3: Effectiveness real but limited: women influenced government through 'moral' sphere → built powerful national organisations → BUT no federal suffrage despite 30+ years

front: How ineffective were women's movements in the Gilded Age?
p1: Union exclusion: male unions refused women's strikes → 1882 Lawrence: no union support → only 2% of trade unionists women by 1900 → AFL excluded women
p2: Class and race: middle-class white women dominated movements → working-class, immigrant and Black women excluded → temperance imposed middle-class values on working-class immigrant communities.
p3: Structural limits: no federal suffrage despite decades → Minor v Happersett (1875) blocked constitutional route

front: How united were women in the Gilded Age?
p1: NWSA and AWSA: despite tactical divisions both pushed for women's suffrage → NAWSA merger (1890): demonstrated capacity for unity → WCTU brought diverse women together → state victories required broad coalitions.
p2: Growing national organisations: NAWSA 2 million members by 1919 → WCTU 300,000 members by 1910 → women's reform network across settlement houses, consumer leagues and suffrage organisations.
p3: United around specific campaigns: Hull House connected middle-class reformers with working-class communities → National Consumer League: cross-class workplace safety advocacy → Women's Crusade (1873): 50,000 from diverse backgrounds.

front: How divided were women in the Gilded Age?
p1: Class: middle-class focused on suffrage and temperance → working-class focused on wages and labour rights → 1882 Lawrence: no suffragist support → temperance was middle-class imposition on immigrant cultures
p2: Race: Black women excluded from NAWSA → Ida B. Wells fought double oppression from outside mainstream → National Association of Coloured Women (1896) required as separate organisation
p3: Tactical: NWSA vs AWSA split over 15th Amendment — weakened campaign for 20 years → 19th Amendment secured white women's vote

front: What were the strengths of women's position by 1932?
p1: Vote secured: 19th Amendment (1920) after 50 years → League of Women Voters educated voters → women 44% of undergraduates by 1930 → ERA introduced (1923)
p2: Growing organisations: American Birth Control League → 222 clinics by 1941 → WTUL advocating for working women → flapper culture — cultural loosening in urban middle class
p3: Political presence: some women in state legislatures and Congress → Women's Bureau (1920) in Department of Labor → League of Women Voters active

front: What were the weaknesses of women's position by 1932?
p1: Suffrage limited: only 1/3 voted in 1920s → Black women faced voter suppression in South → ERA rejected repeatedly → women earned half male wages
p2: Depression (1929): women first targeted for job losses → 80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working → Comstock Laws still in force
p3: Structural inequality unchanged: gender pay gap entrenched → professional barriers to law, medicine, business remained strong → cultural pressure for domestic sphere intensified by Depression

front: How did the New Deal improve women's position?
p1: Perkins: first female Cabinet member → FLSA (1938): minimum wage, 44-hour week, child labour ban → WPA employed 400,000 women by 1938
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt: pushed FDR on appointments → Florence Allen: first female Circuit Court judge → Bethune: led NYA Negro Affairs
p3: New Deal created legal framework supporting later equal pay campaigns → NLRB, FLSA, Social Security established precedent → BUT gender pay gap and women's structural vulnerability fundamentally unchanged.

front: How did the New Deal fail women?
p1: FLSA (1938): female teachers earned 20% less than male in 1939 → CCC excluded women entirely → WPA: one-family-member policy favoured men.
p2: Social Security excluded domestic and agricultural workers — majority of women of colour → 80% Gallup poll (1936) opposed married women working → male breadwinner assumed throughout.
p3: Black women excluded by white-administered Southern relief → Mexican American women vulnerable to deportation → rural women had least access.

front: What was universal about women's experience during the New Deal?
p1: All women faced 80% public opposition to married women working (1936 Gallup) → all excluded from higher-paying jobs or political decision-making → Depression devastated all women
p2: WPA employed women across racial lines — though segregated → Aid to Dependent Children reached single mothers across races — though unequally
p3: CCC excluded all women → gender pay gap universal — whether white professional or Black domestic worker → all women seen as secondary earners throughout New Deal.

front: How different were women's experiences during the New Deal?
p1: By race: Black women excluded from most relief programmes → domestic and agricultural excluded from Social Security → Mexican American women excluded from protections, vulnerable to deportation → Native American women excluded from mainstream networks.
p2: By class: middle-class accessed professional roles — Perkins, Roosevelt, Allen → working-class concentrated in excluded sectors → WPA employed women in gender-segregated lower-paid roles.
p3: By location: rural women — regardless of race — had least access → urban women accessed WPA and CIO unions → Southern women most affected by local white administrators' discrimination.

front: How did Black Power advance Black women's position?
p1: Triple oppression: race, gender and class intersection named → foundational for Black feminism → Elaine Brown: Chairperson of Black Panther Party → Kathleen Cleaver: BPP spokesperson
p2: Cultural reclamation: Afro hairstyle → rejected Eurocentric beauty standards → Angela Davis, Ella Baker: widely recognised → women raised profile of healthcare, education and economic opportunity as Black women's concerns.
p3: Community work: women central to survival programmes — day care, food, health → demonstrated Black women could lead own struggles → Black feminism emerged as distinct intellectual and political movement.

front: How did Black Power limit the position of Black women?
p1: Male chauvinism in BPP: women relegated to typing, cooking, logistics → ideas ignored unless proposed by men (Cleaver) → 'revolutionary first, Sister second'
p2: NOI: rejected birth control → criticised women challenging traditional gender roles → Black Power leaders viewed feminism as 'white women's issue' → focus on reclaiming Black masculinity limited gender equality.
p3: NOW focused on white middle-class concerns → Black women's triple oppression only slowly incorporated → white feminists rarely engaged with racial justice

front: How did Black Power influence the wider women's movement?
p1: Intersectionality: Black Power highlighted race, gender and class intersections → foundational for Black feminism and mainstream feminist theory → militant tactics: radical feminism adopted direct-action approaches inspired by Black Panthers.
p2: NOW pushed — slowly — to incorporate racial justice → Angela Davis, Elaine Brown, Kathleen Cleaver brought revolutionary spirit to feminism → Fannie Lou Hamer demonstrated Black women could lead own struggles.
p3: Tactical influence: fish-ins, occupations and confrontational media strategies all influenced by Black Power → second-wave feminism more militant because of Black Power's example.

front: How limited was Black Power's influence on the women's movement?
p1: NOW and mainstream feminists continued to focus on white middle-class concerns — equal pay and reproductive rights → side-lined Black women's unique struggles → Black Power leaders dismissed feminism as 'white women's issue'.
p2: Radical feminism emerged from broader desire to challenge patriarchy — not solely as reaction to Black Power → NIYC (1961) and other movements showed radical direct action predated Black Power.
p3: By 1992: NOW still predominantly white and middle-class → Black women's vulnerabilities — sterilisation abuse, welfare discrimination — rarely prioritised → intersectionality slow to change feminist practice.
